#4816. The Hidden Cost of Chronic Stress (and 6 Ways to Fight Back)

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 2, 2026 | Reviewed by Jessica Schrader

This is the second post in my series on stress. Read the first one here.

Mortgage payments. Looming layoffs. An upcoming medical procedure. Growing tensions at home.

One worry after another races through your mind on the drive home from work. Just then, your phone rings. A voicemail from your boss: “I need to see you first thing tomorrow in my office.”

By the time you get home, you have a pretty bad headache. Before your partner says anything, you mumble, “I'm really stressed out.”

Generally speaking, stress is a psychological and physiological response to demands and perceived threats that require coping or adaptation.

This “alarm” (i.e., the stress response) can be useful, of course. It helped our ancestors navigate threats to survival: finding food, escaping predators, protecting what they had, and dealing with conflicts in their social groups.

The issue is that this system, which evolved to protect us from threats to survival, is easily and repeatedly activated by modern pressures. It is activated by situations that are perceived as uncertain, uncontrollable, or threatening to things we value (e.g., our finances, health, relationships, etc.): Unpaid bills. Traffic jams. Unanswered emails. Ring. Ring. Ring.

There are two interacting systems in the stress response: the sympathetic-adrenal-medullary (SAM) system and the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis. Yes, that’s a mouthful.

SAM is the body’s fast stress pathway. Only seconds after getting a concerning call from your boss, for example, SAM triggers the release of adrenaline and noradrenaline, which narrows attention, increases heart rate and breathing, directs blood flow toward large muscles, and prepares the body to fight or flee.

The HPA axis, which operates more slowly, controls the release of cortisol, known as the “stress hormone.” Cortisol helps make more energy (i.e., glucose) available for the body to use and coordinates many other physiological changes. These effects help the body cope with prolonged challenges.

HPA and SAM activity are part of allostasis, which is the process of keeping the body functioning by continuously adjusting its internal state to meet changing demands.

Over time, however, repeatedly activating these adaptive systems can produce allostatic load, which is the cumulative wear and tear that chronic stress places on the body.

Thankfully, our bodies also have a way to turn the stress response off. Once a threat has passed, a branch of the autonomic nervous system called the parasympathetic nervous system helps restore the balance. This is the body’s “rest and digest” system. It slows the heart, regulates breathing, and allows your body to shift its focus back to maintenance and recovery.

Typically, the body moves between activation and recovery. The stress response switches on when a threat is detected and then off once the threat has passed. When a stressor is brief and has a clear endpoint, the body can return toward its baseline relatively quickly. But not all stressors are like that.

For many people in modern societies, daily stressors are less about immediate physical threats and more about psychological and social pressures; that is, chronic, low-grade stressors that are difficult to escape:

We go to bed worrying about health, family, finances, and a million other things. Then wake up... and pick up where we left off.

So it appears we have a survival system that is mismatched to important aspects of our environment. Though it protects us in the short term, when this system is activated too frequently or for too long, it can have serious consequences. For instance, it can negatively affect immune function, tissue repair, digestion, reproduction, and many other functions. Over time, these changes can contribute to conditions such as back pain, obesity, diabetes, and heart disease. Chronic stress can affect mental health too, contributing to anxiety, depression, insomnia, relationship difficulties, and alcohol/drug misuse.

We cannot eliminate many of the modern stressors—bills, deadlines, and traffic are not going anywhere. But what we can do is give our bodies more opportunities to restore physiological balance, and prevent the negative effects of chronic stress.

1. One of the best-studied ways to regulate the stress response is exercise. Whether you enjoy dancing, jogging, swimming, or skipping rope, you may find physical activity a wonderful way to not only reduce stress but also increase a sense of self-efficacy and mastery.

2. Nutrition matters too. Eating a nutritious, plant-rich diet may support our ability to cope with stress, although exactly how healthy eating affects the stress response remains an active area of research.

3. Recovery isn't only physical; it's social too. When we feel socially supported, we are less likely to perceive stressful situations as threatening.

4. Walking in nature is another way we can take a break from the sensory overload of our technology-dependent lives. Research has shown that spending time in nature reduces stress and promotes positive feelings.

5. Also consider mind-body practices such as mindfulness meditation, yoga, and tai chi. These can be great stress-relievers. A systematic review found meditation was associated with not only reductions in cortisol but also in blood pressure and C-reactive protein (an inflammation marker).

6. Finally, prioritize sleep. Yes, easier said than done, I know, but it's worth making the effort. Sleep deprivation can heighten feelings of stress and anxiety, making everyday challenges more difficult to manage.

The goal of these strategies isn't to eliminate stress completely, which is impossible anyway and not helpful either. After all, we need the stress response to protect us from genuine threats. The challenge is giving that system enough opportunities to deactivate so we can rest and recover.

In our modern world, the alarm may never stop ringing, but with these strategies, we can help our bodies and minds return to baseline again. And again. And again.

#4815. Ferrari Luce EV starts at $560,800 in the US, $80K less than expected

Ferrari’s first electric car, the Luce, will start at $560,800 in the US, with American deliveries planned for the second quarter of 2027. Car and Driver first reported the figure, and Ferrari has confirmed it.

That’s roughly $80,000 under the ~$640,000 number that has followed the Luce since its unveiling in May, including in our own coverage. But Americans aren’t getting a deal.

Ferrari didn’t give a US price when it launched the Luce in Rome on May 25. It gave a European one: €550,000. Most outlets, us included, ran that through the exchange rate of the day, about $1.16 per euro, and got to roughly $640,000.

The problem is that European car prices are normally quoted with VAT included, and Italy’s rate is 22%.

Take the tax out and the Luce costs about €450,800 in Italy. At today’s rate of roughly $1.12 per euro, that’s around $506,000. So the US price is about $55,000 higher than what an Italian buyer pays before taxes, and American buyers still owe state sales tax on top of the $560,800.

Some of that gap is trade policy. European-built cars now face a 15% US tariff, and Ferrari already raised prices on part of its US lineup last year to cover it. The $560,800 also doesn’t include options, and Ferrari hasn’t published what those cost. Nobody buys a base Ferrari.

None of this will slow sales. Ferrari sold out its 2026 Luce allocation of just under 500 units in less than two months, with China doing a lot of the heavy lifting. In August, the first production chassis went for $40 million at a charity auction for the Ferrari Foundation.

That’s despite a rough reveal. The design, done with Jony Ive and Marc Newson’s LoveFrom, got hammered online, and Ferrari’s stock dropped sharply in the days after the launch before recovering.

The hardware is serious. The Luce uses four motors, one per wheel, for 1,035 hp combined. It’s built on an 800V architecture with a 122 kWh battery pack from SK On, charges at up to 350 kW, and Ferrari rates it at 529 km (329 miles) WLTP. It does 0-100 km/h in 2.5 seconds and weighs 2,260 kg (4,982 lb). It’s also Ferrari’s first five-seater.

For comparison, a Lucid Air Sapphire with over 1,200 hp costs around $250,000. You could buy two and still have change left over.

"None of this will slow sales. Ferrari sold out its 2026 Luce allocation of just under 500 units in less than two months, with China doing a lot of the heavy lifting."

This only proves that the world has too many mega wealthy people with more money than brains. All while the middle class continues to shrink and more people are headed towards homelessness.

The bigger story is that the price clearly doesn’t matter to Ferrari’s buyers. Plenty of luxury brands have convinced themselves that wealthy buyers won’t pay supercar money for an electric car. Maserati killed the electric MC20 Folgore over exactly that fear. Ferrari just put a $560,800 sticker on a four-door EV with a polarizing design and sold out a year of production anyway.

We’re not convinced every one of those orders comes from love of the car. Ferrari’s allocation game rewards loyal customers, and some buyers are surely taking a Luce to stay in line for the next limited-run V12. But a deposit is a deposit.

The real test comes in 2027 and 2028, once the first wave of collectors has its cars and the Luce has to sell on its own merits. Will it?Personally, I hope that the Luce leads to Ferrari trying to make some electric sports cars.

The new series reunites the True Detective duo for some meta sitcom chaos.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

EVERYONE KNOWS THAT Matthew McConaughey and Woody Harrelson are one of the great duos in show business. After meeting and becoming friends on the set of the 1999 comedy film EdTV, the actors began a long friendship, along the way collaborating again for the first season of True Detective, widely considered to be one of the great television shows of all time.

But did you know that in addition to being great friends, the two might also be half-relatives? That’s the premise of Apple TV’s new comedy series Brothers, which reunites the duo on screen for the first time since 2014’s True Detective, and pulls from a bit of very real mythology that the two only relatively recently discovered on their own. “Matthew’s mother, I’d known her 25 years, and she told me, ‘I knew your father.’ You know, like, with the ellipses: ‘I knew… your father’” Harrelson told Variety. “She tells me, and I’m thinking, ‘What’s behind this story?’ And then I find out they weren’t just friends—there was a little more to it.”

Brothers, in turn, stars McConaughey and Harrelson as fictional versions of themselves exploring this possibility. Think of it as the meta-nature of Curb Your Enthusiasm, combined with the goofiness of a family sitcom like Schitt’s Creek or Malcolm in the Middle, and, of course, the star power of True Detective.

Now, just because they made the show doesn’t mean that McConaughey believes the story. “Woody thinks he knows that we’re brothers, and it’s not that I don’t want to know—I don’t believe it,” McConaughey told Variety at the show’s premiere. “My mom’s the one who started this whole damn thing, by saying ‘I knew… your father… with the long pause after that. Even my five-year-old son understood the innuendo of what that meant.”

So, are the A-listers actually brothers? You figure they could just take a DNA test and figure out once and for all. But for now, that doesn’t seem to be in the cards. “I’ve been wanting to, but he refuses,” Harrelson told The Hollywood Reporter. McConaughey then added that maybe that could change in the future—but he’s a little frightened about what it could mean. “I’ll probably come around to it,” he said. “If it’s true, I’ve got a lot to unpack. If it’s not true, he’s not going to be near as fun to hang out with.”

There’s a lot to figure out for these two. But in the meantime, why not see how fictional Matthew and Woody handle it? Below, we’ve got all the information to make sure you don’t miss an episode of Apple TV’s Brothers.

The final episode of Brothers season 1 will officially come out on Wednesday, November 4. But as with all Apple TV shows, it'll release a bit early the night prior. So if you're eager, keep an eye out for the next episode on the evening of Tuesday, November 3.

The debut season of Brothers will run for eight episodes, with episodes rolling out on a weekly basis, the first seven of which have now aired. That means there’s still one more week—and one episodes of Matthew and Woody’s brotherly (or not-so-brotherly) chaos—remaining in the show’s first season.

#4813. Swallowed by a Sea Monster: 'Whalefall' and Fatherhood

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 2, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

One of the best-known stories of the Bible is that of Jonah, a man who gets himself swallowed by a whale (actually, a “great fish”). Why this happens is probably less popularly understood. The reason is that Jonah has defied God. The Lord wanted him to go to the city of Nineveh and preach to the people there about their sins. He refused and sought escape to the city of Tarshish via a ship leaving from Joppa.

As you might imagine, God is not pleased. A storm arises from the sea, and the ship gets dangerously tossed about. When the crew draws lots to determine who is at fault, Jonah’s number comes up. He admits he is Hebrew and has defied God. He volunteers himself as a sacrifice, and they toss him overboard. As expected, the waters become calm.

What happens next is the part most of us know about. Jonah is swallowed by a sea monster. He suffers in “the belly of hell” for three days. Finally, God forgives him and talks to the fish, who “vomited out Jonah upon the dry land.” Jonah goes on to do what he was supposed to do, now wiser from the experience.

This story has burrowed deep into our cultural psyche. Famed psychologist Abraham Maslow found the tale so compelling he came up with a term: the Jonah Complex. To suffer this complex is to fail to follow one’s true calling. You deny yourself, and you will descend into a dark place, where, hopefully, you will realize your errors and return to your true life path. You’ll emerge from the belly of the beast you’d so recklessly volunteered for and find the bright light of day.

In a new movie, "Whalefall," a young man takes Jonah’s original harrowing route. He denies the grief he should be feeling over the death of his father by suicide. This boy has lived a tortured life, marked by a tough relationship with his father. A gruff old salt who’d led scuba tours, dad constantly berated his son for a lack of fortitude and insufficient love of the sea. Father and son fail to understand each other. It is a classic story of the alienation that can arise between “tough” dads and their sensitive sons. The sons feel they are not good enough, and the fathers know they are missing something, but can’t see through their own pain to do anything about it.

The idea that fathers no longer have the tools to raise their sons properly has long been a popular topic in pop psychology. Fathers, we have been told, are emotionally unavailable and do not know how to inculcate in their sons the proper virtues of self-sufficiency and human connection. Sadly, this argument often winds up blaming domineering “viper” mothers who suffocate their sons and diminish their husbands’ role.

"Whalefall" taps the ongoing cultural conversation of finding the father with a wild take on the Jonah story. The boy, on a solo scuba mission to recover remnants of dad (who chose to drown himself rather than wither away from lung cancer), gets swallowed by a sperm whale. The event, wild on its face, is filmed realistically.

Inside the whale, the boy experiences a trip to hell. The space is claustrophobic, the air is poisonous, and his wounds become more and more grievous. In this surreal space, we experience a series of flashbacks that sketch out the father’s failures and the son’s desire to connect with him. Ultimately, the whale itself becomes the father, and through conversation, the boy realizes that his dad did, in fact, love him, even if he could not show it. The whale-father ultimately supplies the boy with the tools to help him escape. Like the Jonah story, he is expelled from the beast to reach the light of day, transformed by his experience.

"Whalefall" offers the metaphorical father redemption arc that delivers a novel take on Maslow’s Jonah Complex. What dad was unable to do in life, he succeeds in doing through a dying sperm whale on the Pacific coast. The boy takes responsibility for his own life success, and the father can finally be properly grieved over. This film, while shot realistically, is in fact a mythic treatment of an enduring social problem. Does it succeed? That depends on the viewer.

#4812. Tesla now says it needs its own maps for FSD after years of dismissing maps

Tesla says it’s building its own maps to fix some of the most common problems with its “Full Self-Driving” system, including reading speed limits, parking, and choosing routes. The company’s head of AI described the effort on Tesla’s Q3 2026 earnings call.

It’s a notable shift for a company whose CEO spent years arguing that self-driving systems relying on maps are brittle. And it shows Tesla’s fleet is now doing the same job Waymo’s cars do: mapping the roads so the self-driving system knows what it can’t reliably figure out on its own.

Tesla fans argue that Waymo’s approach differs because it creates HD maps with lidar, but ultimately both are creating their own maps; if your argument is that Tesla’s maps are less well-defined and needed for driving for different reasons than Waymo’s, you don’t really have an argument.

The question came from Tesla’s shareholder Q&A. A retail investor wrote that mapping “continues to be a problem” for FSD, listing speed limits, parking and typical routes as the three biggest issues, and asked why Tesla relies on third-party maps instead of its own.

Tesla’s VP of AI, Ashok Elluswamy, agreed that “we shouldn’t be depending on external people’s maps.” He said Tesla is building its own maps using a new AI-based mapping and navigation architecture, fed by what the fleet collectively learns, that will also learn individual drivers’ preferences and respond to voice commands.

He said the technology will start handling the beginning and end of trips with FSD v15, and over the following months take over navigation, parking and destination handling.

Tesla has gone back and forth on this before.

In 2015, when it launched Autopilot, Tesla told Fortune it had started building high-precision maps with “100 times the level of granularity” of standard navigation, using data from its customer cars.

At its Autonomy Day in 2019, Elon Musk said Tesla had tried high-precision lane maps and realized it was “a huge mistake.” He called relying on them a “really bad idea” that makes a self-driving system “extremely brittle,” in the same presentation where he called lidar a “fool’s errand.” The message was clear: Waymo needed lidar and detailed maps, and Tesla would solve driving with cameras and AI alone, anywhere.

Seven years later, Tesla is building a map layer from its own fleet to fix the things its vision system gets wrong.

To be fair to Tesla, this isn’t an HD map in the sense Musk criticized. Tesla has always used navigation maps, and building its own instead of licensing them isn’t a contradiction on its own.

But look at the problems Tesla is trying to fix. Speed limits, parking and routes are all about understanding the environment, and FSD still often fails at it, especially with speed limit signs.

Last month, a Belgian road safety group found that FSD sped in 55% of the 30 km/h zones it tested in Brussels, averaging 44 km/h, partly because the car’s screen showed a 50 km/h limit in most of those zones. In the US, NHTSA is weighing an investigation into claims that Tesla Robotaxis speed through active school zones, covering about 1,000 Model Y and Cybercab vehicles.

A speed limit sign is about as simple as road information gets. If an end-to-end vision system can’t reliably read and apply it, and the fix is a better map, then vision alone isn’t doing the job Tesla said it would.

That brings Tesla closer to Waymo than it would like to admit.

Waymo maps a city by driving its sensor-equipped vehicles through it before launching service, and keeps those maps updated as its fleet drives. Tesla is now describing the same idea: its cars collect what they see, and that data feeds a Tesla-built map that helps every car drive better. The main difference is that Waymo’s cars have lidar on top.

It also fits how Tesla’s Robotaxi service actually operates: city by city, inside small geofenced service areas, with Tesla handling the fleet operations. Tesla isn’t talking about centimeter-level HD maps today, but a fleet-built map that keeps getting more detailed could easily head that way.

There’s nothing wrong with using maps. Every serious self-driving program does, and a map built from millions of Tesla cars could be a real advantage. If it fixes FSD’s speed limit problems, that’s good news for everyone sharing the road with it.

Add this as another reason why unsupervised FSD will not be going out to consumer cars in Q2 of 2027. There will be more reasons forthcoming, but not for some time as the main focus will be raking in more cash for those payday goals.

What’s wrong is the years of messaging that Tesla’s approach didn’t need any of this. Musk sold FSD as a general solution that would work anywhere through vision alone, while dismissing Waymo’s maps and lidar as crutches. Now Tesla is adding the map, it already operates in geofences, and the AI still can’t reliably read a 30 km/h sign in Brussels.

Waymo built its maps and has been running a driverless service for years. Tesla is building its maps now and has pushed unsupervised FSD in customer cars to Q2 2027, and only inside its Robotaxi fleet. At what point do we admit that both companies are solving the same problem in very similar ways, and only one of them has lidar?

We are a decade into Tesla’s self-driving effort and it is doing exactly what Musk used to say doesn’t count as a “true self-driving system”: geo-fenced areas using maps.

#4811. Heart Failure Is Becoming More Common in Adults Under 65, Report Finds

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

An estimated 56 million people worldwide were living with heart failure in 2023, more than double the number in 1990, according to a new Global Burden of Disease (GBD) analysis published September 30 in JAMA Cardiology.

Heart failure is a chronic condition in which the heart cannot pump enough blood to meet the body’s needs. Despite its name, heart failure doesn’t mean the heart has stopped beating.

A separate 2026 report from the Heart Failure Society of America (HFSA) found that heart failure contributed to more than 450,000 deaths in the United States in 2023, with particularly sharp increases in mortality among adults under 65.

Approximately 7.7 million U.S. adults (3%) are living with heart failure, according to the HFSA report. That number is projected to rise to 8.7 million by 2030, 10.3 million by 2040, and 11.4 million by 2050.

The GBD researchers said the findings highlight the growing burden of heart failure associated with population growth and aging, as well as the need for prevention and treatment strategies targeting common causes such as ischemic heart disease and hypertension (high blood pressure).

Between 2010 and 2022, heart failure hospitalization rates increased among adults under 65 while declining among those 65 and older. Between 2001 and 2020, estimated heart failure mortality rates more than doubled among adults ages 25 to 44 and nearly doubled among those ages 45 to 64.

“I think we’re seeing the impact of cardiovascular risk factors developing earlier in life. Conditions such as obesity, diabetes, hypertension, and sleep apnea are affecting younger adults at higher rates than in previous generations,” Kevin Shah, MD, Program Director of Heart Failure Outreach at MemorialCare Heart & Vascular Institute at Long Beach Medical Center in Long Beach, CA, who wasn’t involved in the analysis, told Healthline.

“When those risk factors are present for decades, they can eventually lead to heart failure at a younger age,” he said.

Amit Blumfield, MD, a cardiologist at Manhattan Cardiology in New York City who was also not involved in the analysis, noted that improvements in early detection may also play a role.

“Our tools to detect early heart failure are also improving with time, and as a result, patients may receive an earlier diagnosis and can hopefully start medical therapy to prevent progression or possibly even reverse the process entirely.”

Heart failure contributed to 452,573 deaths in the United States in 2023, accounting for approximately 14.6% of all deaths that year, according to the HFSA report.

Age-adjusted heart failure mortality rates increased by approximately 37% between 2010 and 2023, with preliminary 2024 data suggesting the upward trend is continuing.

This increase appears to have reversed more than a decade of previous progress in reducing heart failure mortality.

Ischemic heart disease and hypertension were among the most common causes of heart failure in older adults, according to the GBD report. However, the underlying causes varied considerably by age group and region.

Among children and young adults, congenital heart abnormalities and rheumatic heart disease (RHD) were common causes of heart failure. Heart failure associated with alcohol use was most prevalent during middle adulthood.

The analysis also identified regional differences in the underlying causes of heart failure:

The global burden of heart failure is expected to grow as populations age.

While not all cases of heart failure can be prevented, managing certain risk factors can help reduce your risk. These include:

According to Shah, other important steps to help prevent heart failure include maintaining a healthy weight, staying physically active, and managing conditions such as diabetes and high cholesterol.

He added that regular medical care is important because many of these risk factors can be identified and treated long before heart failure develops.

“Heart failure is often treatable and may even be reversible with early diagnosis and treatment. It is important for patients to seek help early if they have concerning symptoms, such as exertional shortness of breath, chest pain, leg swelling, or anything else they’re concerned about. Talk with your doctors early and often,” said Blumfield.

#4809. The 'Culting' of Mental Health Diagnosis

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 2, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan

The Culting of Brands sounds like one of those polemical books about ad industry manipulation. It’s not. It’s a how-to.

In the early 2000s, marketers were contending with savvy consumers wary of advertising tactics. One marketer, Douglas Atkin, realized that some brands had managed to engender cult-like devotion in their customers that transcended advertising and products.

He studied these "culty" brands and actual cults to figure out how this could work. Cults ensnare smart, capable (and ideally influential) people, he argued, by offering a couple of core human desires: meaning and belonging. Cults enclose a worldview around their followers that pre-answers questions, arming devotees with deeply felt shared perspectives.

His book therefore recommends that brands provide ideologies and identities for consumers. Chapters include “You’re Different, We’re Different,” “You Belong,” “This Is What We Believe,” and “We Love You.”

Another brand strategy book, Lovemarks, asserts that tapping into emotion and helping people to tell the story of their lives through brand values (where disentangling from them would unravel the very story of the self) is key to obtaining loyalty beyond reason from customers.

I write about ways marketing messages have been conflated with medical ones in mental health, and how the emotional affordances of social media platforms enable spaces where we don’t just identify with common characteristics of disorders; we feel them.

Social media is invested in invoking and enlisting user moods, providing and platforming interpretations of those moods, encapsulating them in memes (and sometimes even selling them as user data). Using social media can mimic states we consider overstimulation, executive dysfunction, or dissociation. When TikTok content tells us that “doomscrolling” TikTok is itself a symptom of a disorder and that a therapy app has a solution, we are seeing and feeling content as designed. But diagnostic brands in themselves aren’t new.

A strategy employed by marketers of psychopharmaceuticals has been to sell the diagnosis, not the product. Accomplished through extensive PR campaigns, sponsored conferences, lobbying, screening and awareness initiatives, and other tactics focused on securing an enduring market, the diagnosis becomes the brand (see Healy, 2008; Horwitz, 2021). Product demand follows.

Direct-to-consumer psychopharmaceutical ads often point to a singular explanation for a complex condition—usually a theorized mechanism of a drug's therapeutic effect (a logic roughly akin to assuming social anxiety is an alcohol deficiency). Medication is an important treatment tool for many. Its marketing, however, can discount social, environmental, or even other possible biomedical factors in mental health.

Before medications required association with specific disorders to obtain approval on the market and before there were hundreds of possible diagnoses to link them to, ads in medical journals advised doctors that societal pressures and the pains of living in themselves called for psychiatric medications.

As troubling as some of these ads were (like plainly stating there was no escape for "subservient" 1950s housewives), they did not tend to position anything inherently wrong with people or brains (and drugs like Miltown had a cult brand following beyond being "mother's little helpers"). Today, promotional materials and influencers are more likely to reduce suffering to serotonin, dopamine, or to use totalizing medical analogies (“like insulin for a diabetic”), shaping treatment decisions and self-understanding.

The ubiquitous and scientifically shaky insulin metaphor brings to mind another brand cult strategy, per Atkin, of “shared language.” Social media provides “therapy speak"—a fusion of pop psychology, therapeutic, and loosely applicable clinical terms that structure understanding of ourselves and others.

Clinically, our mental health diagnoses were primarily designed to describe symptoms, not explain them. On social media, however, rather than opening up questions, diagnoses are the answers.

Why does she have these mood swings? Because she’s bipolar. Of course they’re gaslighting me; they’re a narcissist. Why do I feel depressed? I have depression. It’s algorithmically tautological, self-reinforcing, and rests upon frameworks that draw more from PR than psychology or medicine.

Diagnoses and related terms become all-encompassing explanations. Psychiatrist and cult scholar Robert Jay Lifton described “loading the language" as a way of “reducing every issue in a complicated life to a single set of slogans that are said to embody the truth as a totality.” These terms can also work to shut down other ways of discussing, explaining, or exploring our traumas, challenges, capacities, and relationships.

Beyond this, social media diagnosis also provides consumer services and products, as well as the endless scroll of therapeutic information. Promoting a problem alongside a lifelong consumer solution is another marketing staple.

Though loyalty beyond reason is not to specific products in this case, it is to the idea of the diagnosis and the associated worldview its marketing has cultivated. This includes diagnostic lore that arises from social media users themselves; positioning the customer as "co-author" of the brand is textbook marketing strategy.

Who benefits most from these emotionally imbued consumer diagnostic identities? Why do people fervently adopt and "trauma bond" to them? Can they meaningfully improve actual mental health?

I currently research mental health and media. I also teach classes in public relations, advertising, and social media, so I think a lot about this. Something one of my own counseling professors would repeat in class has stuck with me throughout: “Honor the defenses.”

With this in mind, I look at the social media diagnostic identities I write about here and in my book as a way of adapting within increasing demands that include branding oneself in a digital economy. A number of mental health symptoms and associated biomedical components can be viewed as responses that in some way developed to cope with intense stressors.

Finding communities through which to share stories of struggle and healing is a strength of social media and, not incidentally, of social media marketing. The ongoing challenge is to recognize aspects of diagnostic “brand cults” and to continually strive to prioritize mental health over platforms and profits.

Atkin, D. (2004). The culting of brands: When customers become true believers. Portfolio.

Avella, H. (2026). Mood disorder: How social media and therapy tech are shaping mental health. University of California Press.

Healy, D. (2008). Mania: A short history of bipolar disorder. Johns Hopkins University Press.

Horwitz, A. V. (2021). DSM: A history of psychiatry's bible. Johns Hopkins University Press.

Kajanoja, J. and Valtonen, J. (2024). A Descriptive Diagnosis or a Causal Explanation? Accuracy of Depictions of Depression on Authoritative Health Organization Websites. Psychopathology, pp. 1–10.

Lifton, R.J. (1981). Cult Formation. The Harvard Mental Health Letter.

Roberts, K. (2005). Lovemarks: The future beyond brands. Powerhouse books.

#4808. BMW is already discounting the new iX5 with a $1,000 loyalty bonus

The iX5 is set to go on sale in early 2027, but BMW is already offering a loyalty discount to sweeten the deal for those looking to stay with the brand.

Following the new iX3 and i3, the iX5 will go on sale in early 2027 with BMW’s Neue Klasse-inspired design, technology, and sixth-generation (Gen6) eDrive system.

The iX5 is the first fully electric BMW X5. For its fifth generation, the BMW X5 will be available in gas, plug-in hybrid (PHEV), and battery electric (EV) powertrains in the US. Overseas markets will also see diesel and hydrogen fuel-cell versions.

While the gas-powered 2027 X5 40 xDrive is now available, the electric iX5 still says it’s “coming in 2027” on BMW’s website.

BMW is already sweetening the deal with a $1,000 loyalty discount for returning buyers or lessees, according to a memo CarsDirect reviewed that was sent to dealers.

Although a $1,000 credit may not seem like much, it’s twice what BMW is offering for the 2027 iX3. The discount doesn’t require a trade-in and can be stacked with other offers.

BMW’s loyalty discount provides a cash rebate off the MSRP when you buy or lease a new BMW through BMW Financial Services and have owned or leased another BMW within the last 12 months.

The iX5 doesn’t have any other current discounts or lease offers, but keep an eye out closer to launch.

Earlier this week, BMW showcased the i5’s fast-charging capabilities for the first time during a media event in Southern California with IONNA and Alpitronic. During the event, the iX5 60 xDrive hit a peak of 464 kW, which BMW said enables it to add up to 170 miles of range in 10 minutes.

The iX5 60 xDrive uses a massive 144 kWh battery, which BMW estimates will offer up to 435 miles of range.

Powered by a dual-motor all-wheel-drive powertrain, the electric SUV delivers a combined 578 hp (425 kW) and 593 lb-ft of torque, and can go from 0 to 60 mph in 4.4 seconds. It can also tow up to 6,000 lbs.

Inside, the iX5 adopts BMW’s Neue Klasse setup, with a wide 17.9″ central touchscreen and BMW Panoramic Vision that spans the base of the windshield. Buyers can also add the optional 14.6″ passenger screen.

Measuring 197.2″ in length, 78.7″ in width, and 68.9″ in height, the iX5 is about the size of the Porsche Cayenne Electric.

You have to wonder why Tesla’s name keeps coming up in this discussion, too. This BMW has a net battery capacity of 144 kWh and achieves an energy density Tesla hasn’t even come close to matching. Tesla wanted to get there, but the 4680 battery has been a technical disaster. Even the Cybertruck has a significantly smaller battery. On top of that, the BMW is highly efficient, thanks to its electrically excited synchronous motor (EESM), which doesn’t use rare earths. We’re talking about cutting-edge technology here, in a completely different league from Tesla.

BMW will officially launch the 2027 iX5 50 xDrive in the US in the first quarter of 2027, starting at $79,800.

The iX5 is the first all-electric BMW model produced in the US. Production is set to begin at its Plant Spartanburg in South Carolina by the end of the year.

#4806. Viola Davis Says Shingles Pain Was a ‘9 Out of 10’: How It Changed Her Life

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Emmy, Grammy, Oscar, and Tony Award-winning actress and producer Viola Davis was 50 years old and at the height of her career when she developed shingles.

“All of a sudden, I got a rash in the middle of traveling and juggling [back-to-back] movies that started in the middle of my stomach [and] wrapped around my back,” she told Healthline. “And the pain was definitely at a 9 out of 10.”

Focused on work, Davis didn’t see a doctor right away. Her symptoms eventually subsided but later returned on her upper back.

“That is when I was like, ‘Oh, my goodness, I just got bitten by a poisonous spider,” said Davis. “It felt like really bad nerve pain…then someone mentioned the word shingles.”

After seeing a doctor, Davis learned she had shingles, which is caused by the same virus responsible for chickenpox. She also learned that the risk increases with age as the immune system naturally weakens.

“It can also lead to herpetic neuralgia, lifelong pain that can result from a shingles outbreak,” Robyn Liu, MD, member of the board of directors at the American Academy of Family Physicians, told Healthline.

Shingles can affect daily life, including work and sleep.

“Many people don’t realize that shingles can be associated with nerve pain, and for some, that pain can last for months or even years after the rash has resolved due to potential long-term complications,” Jennifer Caudle, DO, family medicine physician and associate professor at Rowan University School of Osteopathic Medicine, told Healthline.

Nearly one in three people in the U.S. develops shingles in their lifetime.

“Anyone who has had chickenpox can get it, but the risk goes up as we age,” said Liu.

After learning about shingles, Davis said she realized that she could no longer ignore her body.

“You just cannot. I mean, I know that people say it at nauseam, but, for me, it meant slowing down,” she said. “But then the shingles slowed me down…even though I was getting up, I was working out, [the] pain and the sluggishness was awful.”

Now 61, Davis has teamed up with GSK for its “Shingles, actually” campaign to raise awareness about shingles.

“[I’m] sending the message out there for women to really honor themselves and honor their bodies,” she said. “Their bodies literally speak. They’re the other character in their lives.”

After her experience with shingles, Davis began scheduling regular annual checkups.

“Before that time, I did absolutely go to my doctor, but only when it was absolutely necessary, you know, to get my colonoscopy, get my mammogram, but I never went if something felt odd,” said Davis.

Now, whenever she feels off, she doesn’t hesitate to see her doctor. She makes it a point to be honest with them about what’s going on with her body, and she is not shy about asking questions.

“I feel that it’s my job. It’s what I owe myself, and not only [do] I owe myself, it’s what I owe my daughter, it’s what I owe my husband, it’s what I owe my elderly mom, who is in advanced dementia [and] I take care of her,” Davis said.

Caudle stressed the importance of bringing questions to your doctor.

“That’s what we’re here for. Sometimes patients ​tell me they don’t realize they can ask questions or introduce a topic that their healthcare provider didn’t bring up first,” she said. “But a simple question like, ‘Am I at risk for shingles?’ can be a great place to begin.”

Davis has made stress reduction a priority. When she developed shingles, she was juggling an intense workload and adjusting to life as a new mom after adopting her daughter.

“I was someone who just ignored stress,” said Davis. “[When] we meet each other, it becomes a contest: Who can work through their stress the best? I felt like I had to strike while the iron was hot.”

Today, Davis makes stress reduction a priority through activities such as spraying her pillows with lavender, taking Epsom salt baths, meditating, going to therapy, exercising, spending time outdoors, using vagus nerve stimulation, and connecting with family and friends.

“It’s like I overdo it now because I feel like I have to overdo it in order to compete with my schedule. But that’s what I owe myself,” Davis said.

Still, her profession can be intense and time consuming due to shooting and promotional schedules. She still makes time to de-stress and focuses on projects that bring her joy.

“Your career is only as important as how much you enjoy it; how much it adds to your life,” said Davis. “[For] me, it used to be something that I felt defined my worth. I don’t feel like it defines my worth now…I feel that I’m already worthy… I was born worthy. That’s how I see it.”

Vaccination is the best way to protect against shingles, Liu said. The shingles vaccine is more than 90% effective at preventing the disease.

“For children, that protection begins with the chickenpox vaccine, which can be given along with other routine childhood immunizations. Preventing chickenpox also lowers the risk of developing shingles later in life,” she said.

Liu recommends two doses of the shingles vaccine for adults 50 and older, as well as adults 19 and older with weakened immune systems.

“Some patients may have more questions because side effects can be more noticeable than with other vaccines, so it’s important to understand the tradeoff: short-term discomfort from the vaccine versus the risk of lasting complications from shingles,” said Liu.

Side effects may include headache or redness, swelling, itching, and soreness where the shot was given.

“I tell my patients that these reactions are common and usually clear up within a day or two. They’re a normal sign that your body is building protection,” said Liu.

#4805. Seattle plans 200 curbside EV charging stations – and you can request one

Seattle plans to add up to 200 public curbside Level 2 EV charging stations by 2030, and residents can now request one near their home or apartment.

For apartment dwellers and anyone who parks on the street, that’s a useful alternative to making a separate trip to charge. More than half of Seattle’s homes are apartments or condos, according to City Light. Older houses and houseboats can also lack somewhere to plug in off the street.

Seattle City Light and the Seattle Department of Transportation are targeting neighborhoods with the fewest charging options.

The chargers are intended for topping up while parked near home. Seattle says its Level 2 curbside EV charging stations can add around 12–30 miles of range per hour, depending on the vehicle and equipment. All the new locations will be open to the public.

City Light currently charges $0.21 per kilowatt-hour at its Level 2 chargers. At that rate, adding 30 kWh would cost $6.30. Using the utility’s estimate of about 3 miles per kWh, that’s roughly 90 miles of range, depending on the EV and driving conditions.

The expansion follows a 2023–2024 pilot at 31 locations, which SDOT says drew strong use and positive community feedback. Seattle’s installations will be funded by the transportation levy voters approved in 2024.

Residents can request a curbside charger through City Light’s program page. Applications will remain open through fall 2027, with locations reviewed and selected on an ongoing basis. The city will consider charging gaps, environmental and equity goals, and whether a site has the electrical infrastructure needed for installation.

#4804. They’ve Taken on Clayface, the Guardians of the Galaxy, and Star Trek. But Can They Survive Each Other?

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

Collin Kelly and Jackson Lanzing are some of the busiest comic book writers in the business—and their deep, complex, and long-standing friendship and working relationship is the biggest reason why.

RELATIONSHIPS ARE HARD. Interpersonal dynamics of any sort require work to maintain—Ben Affleck took a lot of shit for saying his marriage was work, but he was right. A myriad of different factors can destabilize a dynamic between people at any given moment: ego, money, miscommunication, and on the list goes.

Unless you’re Collin Kelly and Jackson Lanzing.

The comic writing duo, collectively and colloquially known as “Hivemind,” have worked on major properties including, but certainly not limited to, Captain America, Guardians of the Galaxy, Star Trek, and Thunderbolts. That’s not to mention their creator-owned work, like the new horror comic, You’ll Never Leave This Place Alive, which is akin to Marvel’s Runaways meets M. Night Shyamalan’s The Village. And right now, their work on the 2022 one-shot Batman: One Bad Day: Clayface, is part of the DNA that makes up Clayface—the latest production from James Gunn’s DC Studios and the current #1 movie in America. These are the kinds of projects that most writers would kill to be a part of. And, at every step, this pair has done it together.

In a profession where it often feels like a Battle Royale-style competition to land a paid gig, how and why do these two decide to work together?

The answer dates back to 2005, when the pair met at the University of Southern California’s famed film school. Lanzing remembers being on his very first film set and passing by a sound guy, David Server, talking about the Avengers. After doubling back and clarifying if he was, indeed, talking about the comic, the pair hit it off. Not long after, Lanzing went over to Server’s place to hang out, where he met Kelly, who was Server’s roommate. “We met briefly and became friendly,” Lanzing says. “I was definitely—let’s say—a little more hubristic back then,” Kelly states. “I think I was a little bit high on my own supply and wasn’t really quite as engaging with other folks as much.” Kelly went off to Ireland to study abroad and “came back and discovered that this guy, [Lanzing], was still in our lives. I really thought it was going to be a short, summer fling.”

The trio would pile in a PT Cruiser lovingly nicknamed “The Beast,” because it would “growl anytime you tried to gas it” and trek down to local comic book shops Golden Apple or Meltdown to pick up new issues for the week. The trio would then go to a greasy pizza place, read their books, and talk about them. “Because we were all film students, we’re breaking apart the story,” Kelly says. “We were really doing our best to effectively just be passionate nerds within the space. Once you spend enough time with someone and see their real passion for something, it's hard not to start to bond. Once you start to see that passion in someone's eyes and understand what they care about, that's how real relationships are built.”

In a way, Kelly’s relationship with Server developed as a Step Brothers-esque “Did we just become best friends” moment. But his relationship with Lanzing had more of the slow-burn nature of a courting.

“It genuinely was,” Kelly confirms. “Absolutely.”

If hanging out and talking shop was the getting-to-know-one-another phase of their relationship, the consummation, as it were, came out of shared vulnerability. The two ended up in a writing group, sharing material back and forth. That’s when they finally read one another’s work, and their perspective shifted. Kelly, who had come to USC from small town roots in both Hawaii and Washington state without much of a plan before the screenwriting program took him in, was similarly moved by Lanzing’s work. “I'm realizing the story he wrote was my experience, he says. “This is a brother, not a foe. Embrace him like a brother. From that moment on, that respect changed the dynamic of our relationship.”

The pair spent more and more time together, especially after they graduated and took a road trip to Lollapalooza to see Radiohead—which Kelly wryly describes as “pots and pans being tossed down the stairs music”—where their respect for one another grew. “I have so much respect for who he is as a creator, " Kelly says. “It's almost like they say, Don't meet your heroes, but it's like, I kind of just get to hang out with one of my heroes all the time.” Lanzing quickly chimes in, saying, “ I just had never met somebody who thought the way Collin did . . . I learned pretty early, not as a writing partner, but as a friend, he filled in a lot of my gaps.”

In those early days, the pair didn’t always have the language to express the depths of their friendship to one another, with both agreeing it was easier to pour that into the work and have it manifest there.

“We were able to have that rich emotional relationship without saying those words exactly because we were able to funnel it all through our characters,” Kelly adds. “We were almost forced by the fact that we had pledged our careers to each other. We were like, the only way we're going to get through this life is together, making beautiful stories together, making things that are tragic and real and sincere. That necessitates us opening up and being real and tragic and sincere with each other in a way that's like, whoa, whoa, whoa, whoa, this is just for the story, man.”

THE AFOREMENTIONED LOLLAPALOOZA trip turned out to be beneficial not only in furthering the pair’s friendship, but giving them a real foot in the door in Hollywood. As they drove from Los Angeles to Chicago, the boys started riffing on story ideas, eventually hitting on their shared love of Akira Kurosawa movies and Japanese culture. On the road, they put together an outline for a movie called Sundown about seven samurai defending a town from Gaki, aka Japanese vampires. “Ultimately, it's about this guy having to kill his best friend,” Lanzing says. “We didn’t really realize we were writing a lot of the early parts of our relationship into the script.”

By the time the trip back to LA concluded, the duo thought Sundown was in good-but-not-great shape. Kelly had a deal with William Morris, and brought the script to his agent there with the understanding that any sale involving the story was now a package deal. While the movie ultimately never got made, it made enough of an impression to get them recurring work, even as the industry shifted in real time, often being tapped to work on web series, which became all the rage after the 2008 financial crisis.

The two worked part-time on storytelling while holding full-time jobs. That schedule meant they’d get together for face-to-face working sessions on Thursday and all day Sunday. “Our wives, our friends, everybody had to accept the fact that, look, if you want Jack or Collin on [those days], you don't get them,” Kelly says.

With such a complicated working arrangement, the possibility of not working as a duo did come up. At one point, Kelly took a chance to co-write an animation with another writer friend, but the production ended up spanning six different time zones. Fundamentally, the project was messing and began taking a toll on Kelly, to the point where it finally came to a head.

“It genuinely is one of the only times I’ve gotten angry at Collin,” Lanzing adds. “That’s the one time I’ve ever had to deploy it in our relationship because it had literally gotten to the point where it was like, he’s disappearing. Not just into this project but into himself.”

Lanzing found it to be the “scariest” moment in their entire relationship. “I think that is legit one of the first times we were ever really emotionally vulnerable with another,” he says. “The crazy thing is, I think it actually brought us closer together.”

“Oh, yeah,” Kelly interjects. “I was scream crying.”

“We lost it at each other and were able to put it back together,” Lanzing says, picking the thread back up. “I think it taught us both, like, okay, we can do this.”

A FEW YEARS ago, DC Comics published a series of Batman-related one-shots. The series, titled “One Bad Day,” draws inspiration from Alan Moore, Brian Bolland, and John Higgins’ seminal The Killing Joke story. In the story, the Joker rolls out his MO, a fitting bit of text that’s become totemic within comic book lore: “All it takes is one bad day to reduce the sanest man alive to lunacy. That’s how far the world is from where I am. Just one bad day.”

The one-shots featured a handful of stories, all told from the point of view of a Batman villain. Kelly and Lanzing’s story, drawn by Xermanico, follows the Basil Karlo version of Clayface, who is on the verge of a breakout role and slowly descends into madness as he kills more and more people in the film industry to get what he wants. It’s also clearly one of the main sources of inspiration for the DCU’s new body horror film Clayface, which released earlier this month to the excitement of DC fans (and landing at the top of the box office). The film follows a version of Clayface named Matt Hagen (Tom Rhys Harries) and his quest for continued fame on the silver screen (even with plenty of body mutations and murders coming along the way).

Kelly says that DC reached out to them specifically because of their Hollywood background—and thought that would be perfect for Clayface. “Talk about taking our trauma and doing our therapy—that book is taking all the pain that we've had and expressing it through the character and taking him through something really genuinely emotional and horrifying,” Kelly says. “And it has nothing to do with being a Clayface.”

But for both men, the book is another kind of cautionary tale. It’s what could have happened to them if they hadn’t found one another. “[Basil] kills and impersonates his supposed best friend,” Lanzing says. “That's the pivot point. That's the thing that makes it not Collin and I's story. Rather than look at the other guy and be like, I want the jobs you have, I want the opportunities you have, I want the talent you have, I want the ideas you have, I want the life you have, I want the face you have. Rather than doing any of that, what we did was we said, What if we take the monetary sacrifice involved in splitting that fifty-fifty, but then do it together and make an alliance that doesn't break, that doesn't lead to one of us stuffing the other one in the back of a car? Does that lead to a better outcome? “At this point, we’re getting to the part of the summit that seems like it led to a better outcome.”

Based on the expansive depth and breadth of their work, the answer is a resounding yes. But in how the two men talk about one another, and their friendship, and what they’ve meant to one another, even without creating together, it’s the kind of relationship anyone would love to have. A perfect partnership where each brings out the best in the other, resulting in something that transcends and goes beyond—even if maintaining and cultivating that relationship can sometimes get tricky or rocky, it’s worth it. Being in a foxhole with someone else is always going to be better than doing it alone.

#4803. Why We Can’t Just Stop Feeling Guilty

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 2, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

It’s something I come across in the consulting room all the time. A client has come to therapy to stop doing something she knows is not serving her. “I need to stop taking her calls”; “I need to stop always picking up after him”; “I need to stop neglecting myself.” So what gets in the way? This is a question I ask a lot. And more often than not, the answer is guilt: “I just feel too guilty when I don’t do it.” And after some probing, the story often goes something like this: If I don’t do what my guilt tells me to do, I’m a bad person, a bad mum, a bad friend, a bad daughter. I’m not who I want to be. If I got rid of my guilt, I wouldn’t know who I am anymore. I’m always the one who takes care of others and fixes things. What if I let go of my guilt and I become lazy and selfish?

I’ve changed my approach to guilt in therapy, and it’s still evolving, but It’s at this point that I used to fall back onto my trusted therapy tools. If this is a belief that is not serving my client, the next logical step is to find a way to challenge it. The problem is that most of my clients know that logically, rationally, they need to stop taking care of everyone else. They know that they need to set boundaries. They even know that they are not, in fact, selfish or lazy because they have mountains of evidence to the contrary.

So why can you not just stop feeling guilty? The question is, in many ways, as nonsensical as asking why we cannot stop feeling anxious or sad or angry. Yet somehow, we have constructed this idea in popular psychology that guilt is something inconvenient we need to let go of. What if we start by trying to understand why you might feel guilty in the first place? Just as anxiety is an emotion that we can never seem to get rid of, it might be that feeling guilty serves a function in our lives that we need to understand. Only then can we find ways to accept that this uncomfortable feeling is unavoidable but does not need to define who we are.

Guilt in itself is what researchers have called a “prosocial” emotion—that is to say, guilt will often motivate us to repair relationships when we have done something wrong. In its purest form, guilt supports cooperation in our social groups. But, just like anxiety can spiral out of control, overinflated guilt that stops us from looking after ourselves has moved far beyond its prosocial utility.

What makes guilt spiral out of control? Researchers suggest that what my clients might be suffering from is “omnipotent responsibility guilt.” The origins of this particular type of guilt feeling can be traced back to our earliest relationships. If a child grows up in a relationship with a parent who is unpredictable or whose feelings are uncontained, the child can learn that it is safer to take responsibility for the adult’s feelings and try to fix them. Children are in a precariously vulnerable state—dependent on their caregiver for safety, regardless of how emotionally safe that caregiver might be.

To keep that caregiver safe in the child’s mind, it can be easier to construct an internal model in which the responsibility for the parent’s happiness is with the child, and the child is to blame if the parent is unhappy. The child continuously fears and predicts relational rupture, and that prediction model grows into adulthood, where it becomes the foundation of an identity in which everyone else’s feelings are more important than our own, and we feel selfish for looking after ourselves.

So, what my therapy tools did not take into consideration, then, is that guilt can be linked to a deep sense of relational danger. Because the story, in fact, goes something like this: If I don’t do what my guilt tells me to do, I’m a bad person, a bad mum, a bad friend, a bad daughter. But if it’s my fault, at least that means I can make it better. And that feels a lot safer than the alternative. Because if I’m not the one who has done something wrong, that means the ones who were meant to keep me safe might not be safe after all. And then the whole world stops being safe.

It can be difficult to make the leap from our present feelings of guilt to our earliest experiences. But the intensity with which many of my clients hold on to their guilt suggests that it fulfills a deep function that feels like survival. By the time we are adults, a tendency to accept responsibility for others’ feelings may have become fiercely intertwined with who we believe we are. We protect ourselves by telling ourselves we are lazy or selfish when we veer off course because, for many of my clients, guilt has become the thing that keeps their relationships, and with that their sense of self, alive.

Tracing this back opens the doors to new therapy tools that can slowly address the impasse so many of my clients can find themselves in:

The reason we cannot just stop feeling guilty is because our feelings are there for a reason. We may not objectively have done anything wrong, but our guilt feelings might still serve a function, even an outdated one that nevertheless keeps us feeling safe. Remember that it is OK to set boundaries, and it is also OK to find it hard. Be kind to yourself and don’t embark on this by yourself. We are social beings who learn safety in relationship, and we need each other’s company to do that.

#4802. BYD is about to launch this luxury electric SUV with 623 miles of range

BYD will open pre-orders for the Denza N8 EV next week, a large five-seat luxury electric SUV with a CLTC range of over 623 miles (1,000 km).

The Denza N8 initially went on sale in China in 2023 as a mid-to-large-size luxury SUV. It was available as a plug-in hybrid (PHEV) with six- and seven-seat configurations.

BYD is preparing to introduce an all-electric version that will deliver the same electric-only driving range as the PHEV did on a full charge and full tank of gas, combined.

“The king of large 5-seater pure electric vehicles,” as Denza calls it, will use BYD’s second-generation Blade Batteries and Flash Charging Technology. The setup delivers “a world-leading 1,003 km pure electric range,” under CLTC conditions, Denza claimed.

BYD’s 1,500 kW Flash Charging tech powers compatible vehicles from 10% to 70% in just five minutes. To go from 10% to 97%, it takes only nine minutes.

Li Hui, Denza’s general manager, announced on Weibo on October 22 that the company plans to open pre-orders for the Denza N8 EV on October 26, with the official launch in November.

Update 10/26/2026: BYD opens pre-orders for the new Denza N8 EV (read more here).

According to a regulatory filing released by China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) in August, the Denza N8 EV is 5,150 mm long, 1,999 mm wide, and 1,820 mm high, with a 3,075 mm wheelbase.

The Denza N8 EV will use a massive 130.15 kWh battery, providing a pure electric CLTC range of up to 623 miles (1,003 km).

BYD will offer a single rear-wheel-drive (RWD) or a tri-motor all-wheel-drive (AWD) powertrain. The RWD version uses a single motor producing either 320 kW (429 hp) or 370 kW (496 hp).

The tri-motor Denza N8, meanwhile, is based on BYD’s e3 platform. The setup includes a 270 kW (362 hp) front motor and two 310 kW (416 hp) rear motors, delivering a combined output of 890 kW (1,193 hp).

Inside, the luxury SUV features two huge digital screens. One 30″ center infotainment screen spans nearly the entire passenger-side dashboard, and a new 43″ (1.1 meter) panoramic head-up display (PHUD) sits below the windshield.

Like many new BYD models, the cabin adopts a minimalist design with premium features like ambient lighting, a three-spoke steering wheel, and higher-end materials.

Ahead of its official launch, the Denza N8 EV was spotted in China undisguised. New images from Autohome show the luxury SUV driving in public, with roof-mounted LiDAR and a sleek, premium look.

Last month, BYD also launched the Denza N8L EV, a slightly longer six-seat version of the current PHEV sold in China.

The Denza N8L EV is available in two versions. The N8L EV Premium starts at 299,800 yuan, or about $45,000, while the Flagship model is priced from 329,800 yuan ($49,000).

Seems Byd launches a new model every month, almost feels like early 2000s GM with 70+ models.

Both versions use a 130.15 kWh BYD Blade Battery 2.0, providing a CLTC range of up to 596 miles (960 km).

The N8L EV is 5,200 mm long, 1,999 mm wide, and 1,820 mm high, with a 3,075 mm wheelbase, or slightly longer than the standard version. It’s about the same size as the current PHEV. The larger SUV features a “208L super-large intelligent electric front trunk.”

BYD will open pre-orders for the Denza N8 EV on October 26, followed by an official launch in November. Check back soon for prices and more details.

#4801. A Former College Athlete’s Battle With Depression

He spent years trying to power through his depression, cycling through several traditional oral antidepressants, before finding a medication that worked for him.

JEREMIAH FELT GLUED to his couch, too sad and unmotivated to move. He was supposed to be getting ready for his wedding—a day when he expected to feel more confident than ever. Instead, his groomsmen had to come to his apartment and help him get there. A former college athlete, Jeremiah was still a big guy, and it took all of them to lift him from the couch and carry him out the door.

It’s not what you think. Jeremiah had absolutely no doubts about marrying the love of his life. He was in the throes of a depressive episode, one of many he had experienced dating back several years. For Jeremiah, becoming a husband meant becoming a provider and protector. But on the day he was supposed to step into that role, he was the one who needed help—and he felt ashamed.

The wedding-day episode was just one part of a much longer struggle. Jeremiah’s symptoms first appeared in college and worsened after graduation. When he entered the workforce, his symptoms worsened and he became exhausted and increasingly apathetic—to the point of neglecting his hygiene. Eventually, he became too depressed to get out of bed in the morning and lost his first job.

In 2012, Jeremiah was officially diagnosed with major depressive disorder (MDD), a mental health condition that can have a significant impact on daily life and make it difficult to find motivation or energy for self-care. Over the next nine years, persistent symptoms made it difficult for him to maintain employment, and he eventually went on disability.

DEPRESSION IN MEN often hides in plain sight. In 2021, 6.2 percent of U.S. adult men and 10.3 percent of U.S. adult women experienced a major depressive episode, according to the National Institute of Mental Health.

Those numbers tell us how common depression is, but not what it looks like. Men and women can experience many of the same symptoms, including sadness, hopelessness, fatigue, changes in sleep, and loss of interest in favorite activities. However, depression often shows up differently in men. Feeling sad or emotional isn’t always the main symptom. For many men, symptoms can show up as headaches, digestive problems, tiredness, irritability, or long-term pain. Feeling isolated or seeking distractions to avoid dealing with feelings or relationships can also be signs.

According to Craig Chepke, MD, DFAPA, a psychiatrist and medical director based in Huntersville, North Carolina, men may have a hard time talking about their feelings and asking for help, making diagnosis and treatment difficult. “Depression in men is often missed or misread, including by men and others close to them, because it doesn’t always look like what people expect depression to look like,” he explains. “Instead of sadness, it may show up as irritability, anger, withdrawal, or self-medication. Sometimes it takes an ultimatum from someone who cares about them just to get them into the office. Depression is a medical condition, not a character flaw, but I hear men with depression say variations of the same thing over and over: ‘If I was just stronger, I’d be able to handle this on my own.’”

Jeremiah agrees. “You feel like less of a man, like you should be able to just power through somehow, or snap out of it,” he says. “But you can’t. You don’t. Depression affects your confidence in every aspect of your life. It becomes a dehumanizing experience.”

BEYOND HIS OWN self-doubt, Jeremiah had a hard time finding healthcare providers who would take his symptoms seriously. He dealt with therapists who minimized his struggles. One provider even attributed his symptoms to restless legs syndrome.

At times, Jeremiah felt that some doctors viewed depression as a “woman’s disease,” subtly calling his masculinity into question. Being a Black man added another layer as he navigated a healthcare system that didn’t always understand his experience.

He experienced more difficulty when he opened up to loved ones. “Being a man is lonely in general. There are very few men you can talk to beneath the surface level about things even though you call each other friends. I shared my struggle with MDD with my two closest friends, and it kind of freaked them out,” he says. “We didn’t talk much after that for about a year.” He received a similar reaction from cousins and extended family members, who weren’t sure what to say or whether to treat him differently. Things improved once they saw that his personality hadn’t fundamentally changed.

Jeremiah’s marriage, however, became a turning point. His wife, a clinical therapist, was uniquely positioned to recognize his condition. Starting around 2016, she began noticing subtle changes, how he would pick up and lose interest in activities and hobbies, and how Jeremiah would withdraw into himself around the house. It was then that she encouraged him to seek professional help. But asking for help was only the beginning. Finding a treatment that adequately addressed his symptoms would take years.

IN 2021, JEREMIAH was diagnosed with treatment-resistant depression (TRD), which affects about 30 percent of people with MDD. TRD is generally defined as MDD that has not resolved after trying at least two traditional oral antidepressants. “By the time someone checks off medication after medication on an intake form, they’ve usually lost something more valuable than time,” Dr. Chepke says of people living with TRD. “They’ve lost hope that anything can get better.”

Jeremiah knew his feelings were real. “TRD is a bully and it will hit you in the face from the moment you wake up,” he says. “Your best days are not behind you. You’re just going through something that a lot of men go through and just aren't able to admit it. You’re working to hold onto the life you want to live, not just your health, but your lifestyle, who you want to be, and the type of man you want to become or already are.”

For a while, Jeremiah kept trying new medications and started losing hope when they didn’t work. But with help from his wife and doctor, he found a different path.

LOOKING BACK, WHAT mattered most to Jeremiah was his wife’s consistent support through the process. In the early years of treatment, she helped him remember appointments and his medication schedules that kept him moving forward when motivation was scarce. Jeremiah’s doctor recommended he try SPRAVATO® (esketamine), an FDA-approved nasal spray for adults with TRD, used alone or with an oral antidepressant.

It is not known if SPRAVATO® is safe and effective for use in preventing suicide or in reducing suicidal thoughts or actions. SPRAVATO® is not for use in place of hospitalization if your healthcare provider determines that hospitalization is needed, even if improvement is experienced after the first dose of SPRAVATO®. SPRAVATO® is not for use as a medicine to prevent or relieve pain (anesthetic). It is not known if SPRAVATO® is safe or effective as an anesthetic medicine. It is not known if SPRAVATO® is safe and effective in children. (Please see additional Important Safety Information including Boxed WARNINGS, limitations of use, and a list of side effects below. Click here to learn more.)

SPRAVATO is only available through a restricted distribution program called the SPRAVATO Risk Evaluation & Mitigation Strategy (REMS). SPRAVATO can only be administered at a certified healthcare setting, and patients self-administer the pre-filled nasal device at a REMS-certified treatment center under direct clinical supervision and are monitored for at least two hours after taking SPRAVATO. SPRAVATO may have serious side effects such as sedation, dissociation, and respiratory depression, and the risk of abuse and misuse.

SPRAVATO represents a different treatment approach for TRD. Unlike traditional antidepressants that work on serotonin, norepinephrine and dopamine, SPRAVATO acts on glutamate, a chemical messenger in the brain that is thought to regulate depression. The role of glutamate in depression and the exact way SPRAVATO works are unknown.

As his depressive symptoms improved, Jeremiah began to engage more with others. He also joined a support group for Black men navigating these challenges. Hearing other people’s stories reminds him that he’s not alone. Today, he works as an IT and cybersecurity instructor in Chicago, speaks at industry conferences, and builds robots in his spare time.

Jeremiah’s experience is his own, and treatment decisions are personal. “There’s no one treatment that’s right for everybody,” Dr. Chepke says. In his practice, Dr. Chepke has witnessed reductions in certain patients’ depressive symptoms when incorporating SPRAVATO into their treatment. While not all of his patients may benefit, seeing some move from repeatedly cycling through different treatments to an option studied specifically for TRD has helped shape how he approaches care for this population.

If you haven’t found relief from your depressive symptoms, talk with your doctor about the options that may be appropriate for you—and most importantly, know that there is hope.

Jeremiah and Dr. Chepke were compensated for their time participating in this article.
