I just ordered the 60v super recycler with delivery on Tuesday. A friend bought one this year and he raved about its dual power button, commercial bag system that throws grass to rear of bagger for complete fill up and full aluminum deck, 3 year warranty. #4713. Letter from the Editor-in-Chief: The Good and the Hard of Life on GLP-1s

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

“Years of diets that worked for a couple of months, then gave all the weight back and more. Now the food noise has gone quiet,” a GLP-1 user shared.

In June, our brilliant News team published a piece about actor Mayim Bialik and her challenging experience with GLP-1 side effects. It did well, like many of the celebrity + health condition + human-interest angle features we create tend to do with our audience (that’s you all reading this!). Not a massive viral hit by any measure, but a strong performer on the traffic front.

Jump forward nearly 4 months; our equally brilliant social media team posts the piece on Facebook, leading with one of Bialik’s quotes from the article: “GLP-1s have helped people in serious need. Of that I am certain. But nobody talks much about what happens when it goes wrong.”

The fuse was lit. Nearly 12k likes, 1k reposts, and 3.5k comments later, the team had their most engaged post of the year by some margin. The irony is not lost on me that Bialik’s quote, about how rarely people talk about side effects, sparked such a deep conversation about that very thing.

GLP-1s are a big topic for Healthline. They drive traffic, they drive revenue, and they offer a rich seam of human-centric storytelling for our teams. Even so, no one predicted the post would catch fire the way it did. Our social team’s read is that a few things stacked up: Mayim Bialik is a name our Facebook audience knows, the topic is one where nearly everyone has a stake, and a busy thread tends to get shown to more people, who then add more comments. That’s the hypothesis. What we’ve consistently seen is that posts that lead with a quote get more people talking than those that lead with a headline. You may have noticed this article takes the same approach.

We also know that the comment sections on social media aren’t always the most hospitable of environments, particularly in the health space. What stood out about the lion’s share of the comments we read was how constructive the discourse was. People were leading with deeply personal and often moving perspectives about the life changing impact (for good and bad) of GLP-1s. In turn, they were met with equally balanced and thoughtful responses.

Many of the comments expanded on Bialik’s experience, detailing long and difficult battles with a range of side effects. But plenty told the other side of the story: years of failed diets and struggles with chronic conditions leading to despondency, side effects that went on to ease with time, and life changing results that were ultimately worth the cost.

The line that opened this piece could have come from any of those commenters. It didn’t. It came from Kitty Hough, who is 75 and lives in London. Eagle-eyed readers will have spotted that she has the same surname as me – that’s because she’s my mom. She’s one of two people closer to the Healthline home who spoke to me for this piece and whose stories echo the Facebook post thread, with the good and the hard bits side by side.

Kitty was a hockey player and distance runner as a girl, the kind who could eat what she liked without it showing. Then came children, and a weight that crept up year after year, with decades of diets that “worked for a couple of months only to be back to my former weight and then some.” In late 2024, after a lot of research, she decided to try tirzepatide.

Since then, Kitty has lost 56 pounds. She says her joints hurt less, which she puts down to reduced inflammation. She is more mobile. The constant chatter about food has faded. She thinks harder before she eats now.

“I am a strong believer that obesity is a disease and in my case certainly not the result of overindulgence or laziness,” she says. “GLP-1s have greatly improved my health and self-esteem. After years of struggling with my weight, I have finally found a way to solve the problem.”

Kitty will also tell you what it cost. Nausea. Constipation. Sulfur-tasting burps and rough nights of indigestion. Initial hair loss that has since grown back, and loose skin. Muscle loss. And she misses some of the true joy of cooking and eating food.

But despite bumps in her journey, Kitty remains convinced that the benefits of GLP-1s for her life and health outweigh any drawbacks she’s experienced. “I am conscious that I will probably be on this drug for a long time if not for life. It is truly a miracle drug.”

I also spoke to Ann Marie Maguire, AGNP-C, RN, TCTCN, a nurse practitioner specializing in transplantation and cellular therapy, the sister of Healthline’s Chief Business Officer Christine Macguire, and someone who has lost over 50lbs since starting GLP-1s in 2022.

“I struggled with my weight since my teens and always believed I should be able to manage it on my own. But in my 30s, my knees were hurting just getting out of bed or walking to dinner. I realized how much my weight was affecting my quality of life. Starting a GLP-1 in 2022, alongside healthier eating and exercise, made a tremendous difference. My only regret is not starting sooner,” said Ann Marie.

As a healthcare professional, Ann Marie also identified cost as a major factor that can’t be ignored regarding GLP-1s and their impact.

“There’s understandable debate about the long-term use and cost of these medications,” she says. “But we also need to consider the health and financial burden of obesity, including cardiovascular complications, hospitalizations, surgeries and ongoing medications. The cost conversation should account for the potential benefits of preventing or reducing those complications.”

Ann Marie points to a frustration many patients will recognize: reaching a healthier weight can become the reason coverage gets cut off. “We don’t automatically stop blood pressure medication because a patient’s readings improve,” she says. The treatment may be what’s keeping the condition controlled. Obesity, she argues, deserves the same approach. “Reaching a goal weight can mean treatment is working, and decisions about continuing it should reflect the patient’s ongoing needs, benefits and side effects.”

It’s important to note that this article looks at the experiences of only a handful of people out of the millions who now take GLP-1s. Like all drugs, these medications are not right for everyone. Side effects are common; some of them can be serious, and both the long-term impact and what happens when people stop are still being worked out. Ultimately, your care team, with knowledge of your medical history, is a far better guide than a comment thread.

Yet the evidence now reaches well beyond the scales: large trials have linked semaglutide to fewer heart attacks and strokes in people with heart disease and slower kidney decline in people with diabetes and kidney disease, and tirzepatide became the first FDA-approved drug for moderate to severe sleep apnea in adults with obesity.

Stories like Kitty’s, Ann Marie’s, Mayim Bialik’s, and those of the 3.5k commenters on the Facebook post aren’t proof of what will happen to you one way or another. But for a lot of people, my mom included, these drugs have changed what an ordinary day looks like, and in many cases changed what their future can look like.

One of the most significant drug developments of the century so far? Hard to argue with.

Robin Hough is the Editor-in-Chief of Healthline, and in addition to this regular Letter from the Editor column, he can be found every other Wednesday in our Healthline Wellness Wire newsletter.

#4712. Battery electric, solar-powered reefer units reach their first customers

The first regular production solar-powered electric trailer refrigeration unit (TRU) in Australia has hit the road with a real customer. Family-owned transport giant Wickham Freight Lines took delivery of the revolutionary reefer just this week.

Refrigerated trailers (reefers) are critical for hauling fresh food and flowers from the farm to your local market — the problem is that they pollute like crazy, powered by high sulfur, red-dye diesel-powered generators that run around the clock, even if the truck pulling them is fully electric. That constant diesel burn spews CO₂ and NOx into industrial and residential areas alike, and contributes significantly to fleets’ carbon emissions and noise pollution at a time when a number of municipalities are moving to regulate both.

It is, as they say, “a real problem,” but Sunswap Endurance cracked it with a solar-powered reefer that can keep food and pharmaceuticals cold in transit without burning a drop of diesel fuel – and now, they have real customers.

One of Australia’s largest privately owned trucking companies, Wickham Freight Lines decided to purchase the Sunswap Endurance solar trailer units following an initial trial, running from Sydney to Brisbane and back this past summer on a route covering a total of 1,670 km (~1,040 miles) over more than 30 hours of driving.

After Wickham’s drivers finished the round trip with over 65% of the battery’s capacity still left, the purchase was a no-brainer.

“I put the Sunswap Endurance into the fleet and told the team to stretch it — treat it as a normal unit,” explains Graham Keogh, director at Wickham Freight Lines. “We were genuinely impressed. I’m a true believer. I love the technology and I’m not a true tech person whatsoever. You can just see that it’s a winner … the performance, reliability and operational savings were beyond what we expected. For a business like ours, running a large fleet across the east coast, with a heavy focus on refrigerated and cold chain freight, this technology makes real commercial sense.”

Sunswap Endurance first showed their new solar reefer unit at HVIA TruckShowX in Hunter Valley this May past. It’s compelling, insultingly simple technology and I, for one, hope this customer delivery is just the first of many. Let us know what you think of these guys, in the comments.

Solar powered refrigeration truck looks like a natural combination. Cost of the solar is offset somewhat by not needing diesel tank, motor, and generator. Majority of savings probably come form not needing constant refueling (fuel + labor), or in not needing to overhaul the engine periodically.

I would be very interested in knowing how quickly the system pays for itself.

#4711. XCMG debuts new, fully autonomous electric terminal tractor [video]

The new XCMG SDA411 concept terminal truck is fully electric, has no cabin, and an L4 autonomous tech stack that’s purpose-built for unmanned logistics – and, if XCMG get their way, it looks like the future of drayage truck operations.

Whether you call them terminal trucks, yard dogs, or anything else, these heavy-duty trucks do work that’s ideally suited to electrification. It’s all low-speed, high-torque, short distance, precision operation, all the time. And the quiet, vibration-free, instant power operation of electric drive is in its element.

Chinese equipment brand XCMG gets it, and they’re taking the electric terminal truck concept a step further with the debut of an all-new, cab-less design that’s 100% autonomous.

“With no cab and an L4 autonomous driving system, the platform is purpose-built for unmanned logistics,” said XCMG, on LinkedIn. “Its 360° perception system enables autonomous navigation, obstacle avoidance, task execution and parking, supporting continuous mixed-traffic operations in demanding environments.”

That same post included a video showing the SDA411 make its way around XCMG’s campus, making some emergency stops, and pulling up to a charger for a human attendant to plug it in (I guess they haven’t heard about Fortescue’s trick with the KUKA welding robot, yet). You can check out the post for yourself, below.

As for the autonomous aspect, while I generally side with labor and humanity over management and technology, there’s some truth to the industry claims that young people don’t want to drive trucks anymore, even with the promise of six-figure salaries.

Combine that with an aging workforce and not enough new talent entering the field, and virtually every industrial sector is struggling with a serious operator shortage. Autonomous equipment like the SDA411 could help address that shortage, keeping goods moving even when there aren’t enough drivers to go around. And rather than simply replacing workers, the technology could let experienced operators oversee multiple vehicles, take on supervisory roles and stay in the industry longer, while making these jobs accessible to people who might not otherwise be able to do them.

It doesn’t have to be autonomous because it’s electric it only needs to be powered by electric motors not gas to be better in every way.

If XCMG get their way, we’ll get to see how that all plays out somewhat sooner than later. In the meantime, we’ll have to settle for hearing what you think about the SDA411 and how it could impact brands like Kalmar and Orange EV in the comments.

#4710. Getting More Physical Activity May Help With Your Perimenopause Symptoms

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

A new study found that exercising more frequently may help alleviate perimenopause symptoms like hot flashes, anxiety, and urinary issues.

The study results were recently presented at The Menopause Society’s 2026 Annual Conference.

Perimenopause is the transitional period leading up to menopause.

Due to hormonal changes that mark the end of a person’s reproductive years, symptoms like hot flashes, mood swings, brain fog, insomnia, and urinary incontinence are common.

Past studies show that lifestyle modifications, such as eating a healthy diet, managing stress, and getting enough physical activity, can help reduce some perimenopause symptoms.

“Physical activity is low cost, accessible, and already known to benefit sleep, mood, and heart and bone health — all areas that matter a great deal during perimenopause,” said study lead and co-author Liudmila Zhaunova, PhD, director of science at Flo Health — the developer of a women’s health tracking app, which was used to collect health data for this study. “But when we looked at the research, there was surprisingly little evidence specific to perimenopause.”

“Hormone therapy isn’t suitable or desired for everyone, so women deserve a broader set of evidence-based options,” Zhaunova told Healthline. “The more we understand about accessible, lifestyle-based approaches, the better equipped women and their healthcare providers are to build a plan that works for them.”

Study researchers recruited more than 1,800 women from around the globe who were using the Flo app.

Study participants were asked to complete online surveys about their physical activity, from not being physically active to exercising more than 5 days a week.

Participants were also asked to report on their perimenopause symptoms in three categories — somatic (body-based issues like hot flashes), psychological (mental health issues like mood changes), and urogenital (issues regarding the urinary or vaginal areas). Researchers rated the severity of these symptoms using the Menopause Rating Scale (MRS).

The researchers found that higher rates of physical activity were associated with fewer perimenopausal symptoms across all three categories.

“Perimenopause symptoms are wide-ranging, and women often experience several at once,” Zhaunova said. “Seeing a lower symptom burden across all three domains suggests that being more active may be relevant to women’s overall experience, not just one symptom.”

Additionally, the scientists discovered that the greatest exercise benefit was observed in the reduction of perimenopausal psychological symptoms.

“Psychological symptoms, such as low mood, irritability, anxiety, and exhaustion, are among the most disruptive parts of perimenopause, and they’re often overlooked or not recognized as related to this life stage,” Zhaunova explained.

“Our findings suggest that physical activity may matter most for mood and anxiety-related symptoms,” she continued.

“This could help women and clinicians have more informed conversations about how to support mental well-being during perimenopause. That said, women with more symptoms may find it harder to exercise, so we need further research to understand the direction of the relationship.”

Sherry Ross, MD, a board certified OB-GYN and Women’s Health Expert at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, said that regular exercise could potentially help relieve perimenopause symptoms like hot flashes and mood changes. Ross wasn’t involved in this study, but noted other benefits of exercising during this life stage:

“Exercise releases endorphins, improves blood vessel health, lowers inflammation, helps reset circadian rhythm, and improves the body’s internal cooling system,” Ross told Healthline. “Collectively, these changes ease anxiety, irritability, mood changes, sleep, and fatigue.”

“There were mixed reviews on how exercise benefits hot flashes, but exercise does help with weight control, which may benefit hot flashes,” she said. “Strengthening the pelvic floor and core may help with the urinary symptoms women many experience in perimenopause.”

Prudence Hall, MD, an OB-GYN in private practice in Santa Monica, CA, and author of “Radiant Again & Forever,” said that building a sustainable exercise routine requires consistency, joy, and community. Hall wasn’t involved in the study, but shared some exercise tips for perimenopausal women.

“Too often in midlife, previously stable women suddenly plummet into deep depression and anxiety, only to be prescribed multiple medications with debilitating side effects that never address the underlying biology,” Hall said.

“While hormone optimization remains essential to correct these endocrine deficiencies, exercise serves as a powerful, non-pharmaceutical therapy that directly targets the true root causes by revitalizing our cellular health and restoring overall vitality.”

#4709. Amflow launches two powerful new electric bikes, including its first SUV-style e-bike

Amflow, the electric bicycle brand that burst onto the scene with some of the most powerful and lightweight electric mountain bikes on the market, is expanding its lineup with two major releases. The company has announced global availability of its new Amflow TL Carbon, while also bringing its removable-battery Amflow PR Carbon series to the US for the first time.

Both models are powered by the latest Avinox mid-drive motor systems, which have quickly earned a reputation for delivering impressive power in surprisingly compact packages.

The biggest departure from Amflow’s roots is the new TL Carbon, which takes the company’s high-performance mountain biking DNA and applies it to a more versatile SUV-style electric bike. While less common in the US (ironically), SUV-style e-bikes are essentially a hybrid electric bicycle designed to act as an all-in-one, “do-it-all” vehicle combining the rugged build and off-road capability of an electric mountain bike with the practical, everyday utility of a city or trekking bike.

Rather than focusing exclusively on technical trails and aggressive mountain biking, the TL Carbon is designed to handle everything from daily commuting to touring and off-road adventures. And with Avinox’s RS800 battery featuring 800Wh of capacity, it’s got plenty of energy on board for diverse adventures.

The full-suspension bike uses the Avinox M2 motor, delivering up to 125 Nm of torque, which should provide more than enough grunt for steep climbs, heavy loads, and just about anything else riders can throw at it.

Avinox e-bike drive systems are known for many things, but chief among them is the extremely high power and torque they offer, eclipsing most other mid-drive motor systems on the market.

Despite that power and versatility, the TL Carbon weighs as little as 22.6 kg (49.8 lb). It also boasts an impressive maximum total weight capacity of 200 kg (441 lb), including the bike itself, rider, and cargo carried on its front and rear racks.

That’s a compelling combination for riders who want the performance of a premium electric mountain bike but need something practical enough to replace a car for everyday trips.

And perhaps most surprisingly, the price isn’t completely outrageous. The Amflow TL Carbon starts at $3,899 in the US and €3,499 in Germany, positioning it competitively against premium European trekking and SUV-style e-bikes.

Meanwhile, American riders are finally getting access to the Amflow PR Carbon series, which had previously launched in other markets.

Unlike Amflow’s earlier electric mountain bikes, the PR series features a removable battery, addressing one of the biggest practical complaints about high-performance eMTBs with integrated batteries.

The new 800 Wh battery weighs just 4 kg (8.8 lb) and can be removed for convenient indoor charging or swapped for a fresh battery to extend a ride. That’s especially useful for riders who don’t have a convenient charging outlet near their bike storage area.

Amflow claims up to 158 km (98 miles) of range under ideal conditions, though that’s based on relatively gentle riding on flat pavement in Eco mode. Riders tackling technical trails with high assistance levels should expect considerably less. But any way you slice it, 800 Wh is a huge battery for eMTBs and should deliver plenty of range under most conditions.

The standard PR Carbon uses the Avinox M2 motor with up to 125 Nm of torque, while the higher-end PR Carbon Pro upgrades to the more powerful Avinox M2S motor, producing up to 150 Nm of torque.

In the US, the PR Carbon starts at $4,999, while the PR Carbon Pro commands $6,799. European pricing starts at €4,499 and €5,899, respectively, based on German pricing.

All three bikes are available beginning today through ⁠Amflow’s official website and its network of authorized dealers. In the US, both models generally arrive as Class 1 e-bikes (no throttle) with a top speed of 20 mph (32 km/h), though Amflow models can typically be unlocked to Class 3 performance with a top speed of 28 mph (45 km/h).

Amflow has been one of the more interesting brands to watch in the premium e-bike space, largely because of how aggressively it has pushed the boundaries of motor performance and bike weight.

But these latest releases show that the company is thinking beyond simply building increasingly powerful electric mountain bikes.

The TL Carbon is particularly interesting to me because it brings that impressive Avinox performance to a more practical platform. As someone who spends a minority of my riding time in the dirt, Amflow suddenly looks a lot more interesting to me, personally. Not everyone needs a dedicated eMTB, but plenty of riders would appreciate a lightweight, powerful, well-equipped electric bike that can handle both weekday commuting and weekend adventures.

And the PR Carbon’s removable battery is a welcome development, especially as the industry continues to recognize that convenience and serviceability matter just as much as outright performance.

With the Avinox ecosystem continuing to expand across more bike brands and categories, Amflow is also facing increasing competition from other manufacturers using the same impressive motors. That makes it all the more important for the brand to differentiate itself through thoughtful bike design, not just headline-grabbing power figures.

#4708. Apple just dropped the AI-oriented M6 chip into the iMac and the 14-inch MacBook Pro

Published Oct 27, 2026 2:14 PM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn more ›

The $899 Mac mini was the first machine to get Apple’s M6 chip back in August, and now it moves into two Macs with built-in displays: the 14-inch MacBook Pro at $1,999 and the iMac at $1,499. Preorders open October 28, and deliveries start November 6. It’s the same 2nm chip in all three, and most of its gains land in on-device AI, where M6 runs two Neural Engines instead of one.

Apple also announced a round of generative tools for Apple Creator Studio, the $12.99-per-month app bundle it launched in January, including Generate Fill in Pixelmator Pro and a beta assistant inside Logic Pro for sound editing. Those updates arrive in November, and a qualifying new Mac comes with three months of the subscription free.

M6 has a 12-core CPU and a 12-core GPU, two more cores apiece than the base M5. Apple claims the chip has the world’s fastest CPU core, but that’s for real-world benchmarks to decide. The bigger architectural change is the Neural Engine. M6 runs two 16-core Neural Engines, and Apple rates the pair at up to 1.9x faster than the single engine in M5.

Every GPU core still carries a Neural Accelerator, the M5 addition that lets the graphics hardware take on AI work. Memory bandwidth reaches 170GB/s on configurations with 24GB or more, while 16GB models stay at 153GB/s, the same as M5. That gap matters for local language models, whose weights move through memory for every token they generate, so anyone planning to run them should budget for the memory upgrade.

The footnotes in Apple’s MacBook Pro announcement show who the company is selling to. Against an M5 MacBook Pro, Apple’s Blender, Xcode, and Affinity tests come in between 1.2x and 1.3x faster, and so does time to first token in a local language model. Against a 13-inch MacBook Pro with M1, the same Blender render runs up to 11.7x faster. Consider this a nudge to anyone clinging to a computer bought at the dawn of COVID.

The new MacBook Pro costs the same $1,999 as the M5 model it replaces. That’s still $300 more than the M5 version cost when the M5 Pro and M5 Max MacBook Pros arrived in March, because Apple raised the 1TB MacBook Pro from $1,699 to $1,999 in June and attributed the jump to a memory chip shortage. Storage starts at 1TB, and memory starts at 16GB with a 32GB ceiling.

Wireless gets the upgrade the M5 Pro and M5 Max received earlier this year, moving to Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6. The ports stay put, with three Thunderbolt 4 ports, HDMI, MagSafe 3, an SDXC slot, and a headphone jack. Thunderbolt 5 still requires stepping up to an M5 Pro model, which Apple continues to sell alongside the new one.

Apple rates the M6 model at up to 24 hours of battery life and says it runs at the same speed unplugged as it does on the charger. It can reach 50 percent in 30 minutes with a higher-wattage USB-C adapter, such as Apple’s 96W model. The Liquid Retina XDR display peaks at 1,600 nits for HDR, and a nano-texture option cuts glare for anyone who works next to a window. It comes in space black and silver.

If you’re familiar with the MBP already, there are no huge surprises here, just the inevitable march ahead in terms of hardware. That’s not a bad thing.

On the outside, the iMac’s spec sheet reads like the M4 model’s. It has a 24-inch 4.5K Retina display rated at 500 nits, a 12MP Center Stage camera, and seven colors running from blue to orange. Apple says M6 brings up to 5x faster on-device AI than the M4 iMac, up to 2x the ray-tracing performance in games, and SSD reads and writes up to twice as fast. You should feel the upgrade, but it’s not a revolution.

The $1,499 iMac has a 10-core CPU and a 10-core GPU. Spending $1,699 gets the 12-core chip plus all four Thunderbolt 4 ports, 2.5 Gigabit Ethernet, a Magic Keyboard with Touch ID in the box, and access to the nano-texture display option. On the M4 iMac, the 10-core model already came with four Thunderbolt ports and a Touch ID keyboard.

The 2.5 Gigabit Ethernet port is the sleeper upgrade for anyone who keeps a photo or video library on a network drive, and Apple rates it at up to 2.5x the wired speed of the previous iMac. Both models move to Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 and can drive up to two 6K external displays. Every iMac still ships with a color-matched keyboard and a mouse or trackpad, all of which charge over USB-C.

Apple Creator Studio bundles Final Cut Pro, Logic Pro, Pixelmator Pro, Motion, Compressor, and MainStage into one subscription, with exclusive extras for Keynote, Pages, Numbers, and Freeform. The November update leans hard on generative tools. Pixelmator Pro gets Generate Fill, which lets you circle part of an image, describe the change, and have the app match the lighting, perspective, and texture around it.

Final Cut Pro and Motion add text-to-image generation inside projects, and both can send an image to Pixelmator Pro and pull the edits back into the project. Final Cut Pro also picks up built-in MotionVFX effects and titles, rotoscoping and tracking tools, and 23 new transcription languages. Compressor learns to encode Cinematic mode video from the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo. If that doesn’t mean anything to you, don’t worry. Apple does a good job making the software accessible while still letting pros have their complex features.

Logic Pro’s new assistant runs in beta on the Mac only, and Apple says it’s built on Apple’s own models and OpenAI’s. It requires macOS 27 on an Apple Intelligence-capable Mac and works in U.S. English for now. The Stem Splitter may be the more immediately useful change, since it can now isolate, replace, or rebalance individual drum parts.

If you’re still carrying an M1 laptop, Apple built its benchmark footnotes for you. The base configuration pairs the 12-core M6 with 16GB of memory and a 1TB SSD, and Apple rates the battery at up to 24 hours. Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 are new to this tier, while the three Thunderbolt 4 ports, HDMI, and SDXC slot carry over unchanged.

Spend the extra $200 if you can. The $1,699 iMac adds the 12-core M6, all four Thunderbolt 4 ports, 2.5 Gigabit Ethernet, and a Touch ID keyboard, which covers most of what separates this generation from the last. The 24-inch 4.5K display and seven colors carry over, and the 10-core model at $1,499 is the cheapest M6 Mac that comes with a screen.

Buying Final Cut Pro and Logic Pro outright costs $499.98, which covers nearly four years of this subscription at the $129 annual rate. The bundle adds Pixelmator Pro, Motion, Compressor, and MainStage on top, and Family Sharing extends it to up to six people. Students and educators pay $2.99 per month after verification, though their plans can’t be shared.

#4707. China’s super-secret space plane visible in clearest photo yet

Published Oct 27, 2026 2:51 PM EDT

The Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA) has released the public’s best look yet at Shenlong, China’s ultra-secret space plane. Details remain scarce on the experimental reusable vehicle, but the unclassified photo offers an unprecedented glimpse of the craft from below, as well as clear views of its unique, rear-facing solar panel arrays.

The photo was taken in 2024 by the geospace intelligence company Maxar Technologies, and is wedged inside the DIA’s latest edition of its Challenges to Security in Space report. The 130-page threat assessment examines the biggest space-based issues currently facing the U.S. and its allies. Although the ever-growing cloud of orbital debris and junk above everyone’s heads remains an international problem, the report also focuses on the near- and long-term aims of countries like China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea.

Located on page 53 of the report, the photo’s caption simply describes it as an unnamed Chinese “spaceplane,” but it is almost certainly China’s second reusable orbital vehicle, Shenlong. Very little is known about the project even nearly 20 years after China officially revealed its existence. A Shenlong prototype launched on an initial two-day orbital mission in 2020, followed by a 276-day mission in 2022. Maxar’s 2024 photo coincides with the country’s third known, 268-day orbital test of Shenlong that launched in December 2023. According to the DIA, Shenlong “released and interacted with an object,” but good luck learning much else about it.

The mysterious space plane is reportedly engaged in a fourth excursion after launching from China’s Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center on February 7, 2026. This places it alongside X-37B, the U.S. Space Force’s own secretive robot plane. Designed by Boeing, the reusable vehicle has spent 431 days and counting in low Earth orbit on its eighth classified mission. There is also a bit more available information on the solar-powered spaceplane. The vertical takeoff, horizontal-landing spaceplane measures over 29 feet long, features a nearly 15-foot-long wingspan, and reaches an orbital speed of 17,426 mph. Its full capabilities are unsurprisingly highly classified, although the U.S. Space Force did reveal its eighth mission includes testing cutting-edge laser communications technology as well as quantum measurement instruments.

#4706. All aboard! Massachusetts is getting 10 new electric transit trains

The Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority (MBTA) board of directors voted unanimously Thursday to approve the purchase of a new generation of battery-powered public transit trains – and they can’t arrive soon enough.

“(MBTA) has, obviously, an immediate need for locomotives,” explains William Wolfgang, the MBTA’s senior director of vehicle engineering. The new machines will replace the oldest locomotives in the MBTA fleet, GP40s built more than 50 years ago and F40s that are well over 30 years old. In a presentation to the MTBA board, MTBA said 13 of the GP40s have, “exceeded their useful life,” while the F40s will reach the end of their life between 2029 and 2035.

The MBTA will put in an order for 20 Siemens-built “Charger” locomotives; 10 Tier 4 diesel-powered hybrid electric units and 10 dual-mode battery/catenary electric units – and, beyond trackside power for charging the batteries, there are other challenges presented by going electric, most notably using existing cab cars to control the battery-electric units. “We’re going to have to work with railroad operations, engineering, and the Brotherhood of [Locomotive Engineers and Trainmen] to try and determine the best way to handle that,” adds Wolfgang. “That will be an upcoming change order once we get into the design review process.”

The total bill comes out to $310.4 million. A combination of state and federal funding will pay for the order, including a recent $200 million transfer from the Massachusetts Department of Transportation.

The contract includes an option for additional locomotives, although details were not discussed during the meeting. Delivery of the new Siemens Charger trains is set to begin in 2029, with all 20 set to be in service by the end of 2030. Siemens has delivered 440 Charger model hybrid- and battery-electric locomotives globally at the time of this writing.

#4705. The Absolute Best Lego Car Sets for Gifting

Our car experts choose every product we feature. We may earn money from the links on this page.

Lego car sets brilliantly celebrate beloved automotive designs, and there’s a set that’s perfect for every enthusiast on your list. Here are our editors’ favorite picks from among Lego’s top sellers.

This article was updated with new products and information in October 2026.

Lego is a timeless brand, and for those who are collectors, its treasures are so much more. For almost 100 years, Lego has made not just toys but pieces of pop-culture iconography. This, of course, includes cars and other vehicles that celebrate both auto manufacturers and Lego’s flawless designs.

Lego car sets offer gearheads the chance to build their dream machines one brick at a time.

Whether you’re constructing a supercar, an off-road beast, or a Formula 1 machine, these sets capture the essence of legendary vehicles with impeccable detail and mechanical functions that mimic the real thing. Not only do they deliver hours of challenging entertainment, but they also give you a stunning display-worthy model once complete. If you’ve ever dreamed of owning a Porsche, a Ferrari, or an Aston Martin, here’s your chance—no license or garage required.

Ferrari’s 488 Pista gets the Technic treatment with this 882-piece re-creation of the Italian supercar. Finished in signature Ferrari red with racing stripes, the model features a working V-8 engine with moving pistons, a differential, functional steering, and opening doors and hood. Technic sets do require some patience, but for seasoned collectors, it’s well worth it.

Bonus for gamers: The set includes a code to unlock a special livery in Forza Horizon 6.

Koenigsegg builds some of the world’s most outrageous hypercars, and Lego’s 4104-piece Sadair’s Spear brings that engineering obsession to your home. This massive Technic model features a working nine-speed transmission, moving V-8 pistons, functional steering, and intricate triplex suspension. The real standout is its Ghost mode, which simultaneously opens the doors and hood while folding the mirrors. Measuring nearly two feet long, it’s an ambitious build for true enthusiasts.

F1 Academy is bringing more women into motorsport, and this season, the all-female racing series has its own Lego Speed Champions set to match the car on track. This 201-piece build re-creates the Lego-sponsored car from tail to wings, including its colorful livery. It also includes driver Esmee Kosterman as a minifigure. It’s a quick build, but the attention to detail makes it really pop even at this small size.

For the Bronco fan who’s always plotting the next trail, this 943-piece Technic build brings off-road attitude to the workbench. The rear spare tire steers the model, the hood lifts to reveal a V-6, and the suspension moves. A gift with enough real-car flavor to earn a spot on the shelf.

Few sports cars are as recognizable as the Porsche 911, and Lego knows this. This set captures its timeless design beautifully. Complete with its signature whale-tail spoiler, it even has a removable roof. This 1458-piece set features working steering, a detailed interior, and a rear-mounted flat-six engine. With plenty of clever details, it deserves a spot on any Porsche enthusiast’s shelf.

For the F1 fan who still thinks about race day on Monday, Lego’s 251-piece Oracle Red Bull Racing RB20 is a satisfying little garage project. Build a brick version of Red Bull’s 2024 F1 car, then park it on a desk or shelf with its own driver minifigure.

Great Scott, this one comes with options: Lego’s 357-piece Back to the Future Time Machine builds as the DeLorean from the first movie, lightning rod and all, then rebuilds into its flying version with sideways wheels and Mr. Fusion. Doc Brown and Marty McFly minifigures ride along. A gift that’s fun to build and just as good on display.

Ferrari’s SF90 XX Stradale is re-created in Lego form with this 339-piece set. It captures the car’s sharp angles, aggressive aero, rear wing, twin tailpipes, and signature Ferrari wheels, plus it includes a Ferrari-suited driver minifigure. This is a compact build that works for first-timers and experts alike.

The Technic Mercedes-Benz G500 is a nearly 3000-piece build modeled after the iconic G-wagen. It features a working suspension, a detailed V-8 engine, and an authentic chassis that reflects the real SUV’s off-road capability. It’s a substantial build that highlights Mercedes-Benz craftsmanship.

Road & Track has chronicled the Hoonicorn’s starring role in Ken Block and Hoonigan’s Gymkhana films; now you can build the tire-smoking ’65 Mustang from Lego pieces. This 345-piece Speed Champions set includes Block’s No. 43 car and a Ken Block minifigure. It’s a fitting gift for Gymkhana fans, gearheads, and anyone who still misses seeing him drive.

The Jaguar E-type is widely considered one of the most beautiful cars ever built, and Lego’s 1673-piece re-creation makes a convincing case for why. Finished in classic British Racing green, this model captures the E-type’s unmistakable long hood, sweeping curves, and wire-style wheels. Lift the hood to reveal a detailed inline-six engine. There’s even working steering and a miniature tool kit tucked into the trunk. It’s a gorgeous display piece for anyone who appreciates British motoring.

A fan favorite since its release, the Technic Porsche 911 GT3 R captures AO Racing’s instantly recognizable Rexy livery. The 1313-piece set delivers serious detail, including four-wheel independent suspension, rear-wheel drive with a differential, a six-cylinder boxer engine with correct firing order, synchronized airjacks, and opening doors. It’s a faithful, function-forward build that mirrors the real race car’s engineering and attitude.

Ferrari’s 2004 Formula 1 season was legendary, with Michael Schumacher claiming 13 victories on his way to a seventh world championship. Lego celebrates that dominance with this 735-piece re-creation of the Ferrari F2004, complete with working steering, grooved Bridgestone tires, and a detailed V-10 engine. The set also includes a Schumacher minifigure with its own display podium. This is the perfect gift for any F1 fan.

Toyota’s GR Supra brings modern Japanese sports-car appeal to Speed Champions, which re-creates the fifth-generation car in bright yellow, complete with its distinctive front end, sculpted bodywork, and sporty rear spoiler. The wider eight-stud chassis fits a two-seat cockpit for a little extra personality. At just 299 pieces, it’s a solid pick for JDM enthusiasts.

The 771-piece Bugatti Pur Sport captures the orange and black styling in a compact Technic build. It includes working steering, a detailed W-16 engine, and opening doors and hood. This is a very hands-on set that is worth the hours put in.

Few helmets in motorsport history are as recognizable as Ayrton Senna’s. Lego pays tribute to the three-time Formula 1 world champion with this 931-piece replica. The set also includes a Senna minifigure wearing a Senninha T-shirt. It’s a fitting tribute to one of racing’s greatest legends.

Give the car enthusiast in your life a hypercar they can build by hand. Designed for builders ages 10 and up, it features an articulated V-8, working steering, and dramatic doors that swing outward and rotate 90 degrees. It’s a hands-on gift with real engineering under the hood.

Aston Martin’s signature green looks fantastic in Lego form. This 1/8th-scale re-creation of the AMR25 Formula 1 car features working steering, front and rear suspension, a detailed V-6 engine, and a two-speed gearbox. There’s even a functioning DRS system that raises the rear wing when you shift into high gear. Measuring 24 inches long, it’s an impressive display piece with 1547 pieces. Fernando fans, clock in: This one is worth the time.

Audi is the new F1 addition to their Speed Champions group. The 216-piece set captures the team’s striking silver, black, and red livery, complete with sponsor logos. The design even reflects F1’s updated 2026 regulations. A great way to commemorate Audi’s first Formula 1 season.

The Ferrari 499P is a celebration of Ferrari’s return to the top class of endurance racing, which delivered three consecutive Le Mans victories from 2023 to ’25. The 329-piece Speed Champions set celebrates that success. These prototype cars have a distinctive low-slung cockpit, a prominent rear wing, a roof-mounted air intake, and Michelin-branded tires. It’ll be a standout against your other Lego sets.

Few supercars capture the excess of the Eighties quite like the Lamborghini Countach. There’s plenty of nostalgia in this 262-piece set. Finished in classic white, this model captures the Countach’s unmistakable wedge-shaped body, angular styling, and dramatic rear wing. It makes an especially fun addition for fans of vintage Italian supercars.

When buying a Lego car set, there are a few factors to consider. Sets range from beginner-friendly options to extremely advanced builds for the über-experienced. Choosing a complexity that matches your skill set or that of the person you’re buying for is important.

Think about the purpose of the set too. Is this a one-and-done way to spend an afternoon? Is this build going to be several long sessions? Will this be a decoration serving as a centerpiece in an office or living room? If so, picking a visually stunning set will rank higher for you.

Budget will also determine what kind of set you pick. Premium options offer more details but cost more money.

Lego car sets vary widely in complexity, catering to many skill levels. Beginners can enjoy the simpler, smaller Speed Champions and Icons sets. Intermediate builders might prefer larger Creator 2in1 models, which introduce a bit more intricacy than a starter kit.

For a true challenge, expert-level builders might prefer advanced Technic sets. These offer highly detailed replicas of beloved supercars and hypercars, often with features like working suspensions. They’ll also have more complex moving parts such as gearboxes and engine pistons. However, patience and precision are definitely required.

A small Speed Champions set is ideal for an easy way to pass a quiet afternoon. If you want more authenticity, the Technic supercars offer realistic designs that pop wherever they’re placed.

Fans of certain manufacturers may seek Lego collaborations with luxury-car brands, which often gain value over time. Those focused on the building experience will enjoy the satisfaction of the process and the finished result. At the same time, Lego car sets also make versatile gifts, especially if you know the recipient is an admirer of, say, Porsche or Mercedes.

Simpler quick models ($10–$20) will be easy and affordable. Midrange sets ($20–$60) add a little extra realism and functionality. High-budget options ($60–$150) push the features, details, and playability. Premium sets ($150+), such as the Technic supercars, offer lifelike builds, making them great gifts for collectors. Limited-edition models ($200+) are not only valuable to collectors but also pieces of artwork when completed. Matching your budget to your desired experience ensures you get the best value.

The top Lego car sets for display include Technic supercars, Speed Champions, limited-edition models, and custom builds. The Technic line offers so many gorgeous designs that they will impress even those without engineering knowledge. The smaller and easier Speed Champions line has just as stunning branded collaborations. Each caters to different display preferences, from realism and brand prestige to compactness and style in both collections.

Lego car sets can increase in value over time, particularly if they are rare or limited editions. Factors influencing value appreciation include the condition of the set—new, sealed boxes generally hold more value—along with popularity and demand for specific models. Nostalgic connections to certain cars can also drive up interest among collectors.

Lego car sets are suitable for both kids and adults, but you should take into account skill level and piece sizes. Some sets, featuring bigger and fewer pieces, are designed specifically for young builders. Adult builders will gravitate toward more intricate models.

Yes, Lego car sets can be combined for custom builds, allowing builders to mix and match pieces from different sets to create unique vehicles. This encourages creativity and innovation for younger builders. Many Lego enthusiasts share their custom creations online at sites like Lego Ideas, offering inspiration and ideas for others.

#4704. Why are bogs so good at preserving dead bodies?

Published Oct 27, 2026 3:43 PM EDT

In August of 1984, commercial peat cutters working near Wilmslow, about a half-hour drive south of Manchester, England, discovered a dead body in the moss. The corpse was determined to be a 25-year-old man with a closely shorn beard and well-manicured nails. He had suffered two or three heavy blows to the head, and had sustained a cut throat and a fractured rib. But this wasn’t a fresh corpse: His body had been laying in that peat bog for nearly 2,000 years.

The “Lindow Man” is just one of at least 2,000 bog bodies recovered from Europe’s peatlands. They date from the Mesolithic period, which ended in Europe between 8,500 to 5,500 years ago, all the way up through World War II.

“Bog bodies” are essentially human corpses that peat bogs have naturally preserved and mummified. Quite often, their skin, hair, nails, and internal organs are remarkably intact for thousands of years. Their bones, however, are a whole other story.

To find out more about why bogs are so good at preserving bodies, Popular Science turned to author Anna North, a journalist whose fascination with peat bogs and preserved “bog bodies” inspired her national bestseller Bog Queen. This eco-historical mystery novel details what happens when a forensic anthropologist starts investigating a well-preserved Iron Age bog body, and required extensive research on North’s part. The author first got the idea for her book after coming across the Lindow Man at London’s British Museum, where he’s on permanent display.

“He doesn’t look great,” she says, “but he’s just so recognizably still a human.” The fact that North was sharing a room with this person who ate, drank, and walked the earth 2,000 years ago left an indelible mark on her. She wanted to learn more. “One of the first things I realized is that I didn’t have a good sense of what a peat bog would even look like.”

A bog or “peat bog” is an acidic, nutrient-poor wetland ecosystem. It’s made up of peat, which is ground that’s soft and spongy and consists of partially decayed plant material that builds up over hundreds or thousands of years.

“Peat is really any kind of organic matter that builds up faster than it decays,” says North. It can be grasses, reeds, roots, and shrubs. But peat mostly consists of Sphagnum moss, a large group of shaggy-looking, moisture-loving mosses.

“Sphagnum moss has the capacity to take in a lot of water and store it, so it becomes really spongy and waterlogged.” This creates an excellent environment for preservation, says North, “because there’s not much air.”

While bogs exist across the globe, you’ll find them mostly in cool, northern climates with lots of rain. For years, these mysterious landscapes have appeared as ominous settings in literature. They’re especially popular in Victorian detective fiction and gothic novels like Sir Arthur Conan Doyle’s The Hounds of the Baskervilles and Daphne du Maurier’s Jamaica Inn. And for good reason. Their mist-shrouded surfaces (a result of the cool, damp air that sits above their spongy terrain), unstable footing, and stagnant waters make them natural backdrops for the unknown. Of course, there are also the bodies.

The preservation of bog bodies results from a highly-detailed balance of water source, chemistry, and vegetation.

Bogs get almost all of their water from rain and snow, which makes them low in minerals and nutrients. The water also doesn’t move thanks to the bog’s sponge-like moss.

Thick layers of decomposed organic material choke off the air supply to the decaying plant matter underneath. Without oxygen, the environment becomes highly acidic and aerobic bacteria and fungi are unable to thrive. This means they can’t break down that dead plant (and human) material the way they normally would.

Instead, the bog’s high acidity essentially “pickles” human corpses, many of which were left behind as part of a ritual sacrifice or the result of executions. The environment’s low pH (the result of its high acidity) acts like a pickle juice brine, stopping harmful bacteria from growing and preserving bodies almost like “living time capsules.” Sphagnum moss also releases a complex carbohydrate that binds to the proteins in human skin and tissue, called sphagnan. This carbohydrate turns the skin leathery and a dark-brown “tea” color while protecting it against decay. But while this unique environment slows a body’s decomposition, the bog’s intense acid leaches the calcium right out of human bones.

“If you look at X-rays of bog bodies, they’re not going to look like an X-ray of a living person,” says North. Mostly because the bones are softened, warped, or have dissolved completely.

Raised bogs, which are deep, dome-shaped peatlands that are both wetter and higher than their surrounding lands, are best at preserving bodies. That’s because they’re both highly acidic and entirely void of oxygen.

The shallower peat found in blanket bogs means that bodies decompose faster (though bog bodies are still found here). Fens, which are peat-accumulating wetlands that both  surface water and mineral-rich groundwater replenish, are less acidic. This means that a body’s soft-tissue will typically decay.

One way that forensic anthropologists can typically tell the difference between a recently decreased person and a bog body is through their teeth. While researching for her book, North discovered that people who lived and died before there was refined flour would have really different patterns of tooth decay than modern-day eaters.

Back then, she says, “They might actually grind wheat or corn with stone, and little bits of stone would end up in their flour. Those people would then chew on that stone and it would grind down their teeth.”

Cremation or casket? Here’s the most eco-friendly burial option.

What happens when you donate your body to science?

How human composting turns bodies into soil

Some people really are werewolves—at least, in their minds

What happens to your body when you die in space?

North also learned that identifying a bog body is a collaborative effort. A bioarchaeologist, who studies human biological remains at archaeological sites, might be brought in to determine the corpse’s age and sex, while a pathologist would examine the cause of death.

“It turns out that the same process that makes bogs really good at preserving a body also means that they’re storing this enormous amount of carbon,” says North.

Since there’s no oxygen to break down a bog’s organic plant matter, it just piles up layer by layer forming thick, carbon-rich peat. In fact, peatlands (including bogs) only cover roughly three-perfect of the planet’s land surface, though they store twice as much carbon as all the world’s forests combined. “They’re just a really powerful resource.”

Bogs are generally safe to walk across as well, despite their reputation for being “graveyards” of sorts. “There are cases of people appearing to have accidentally died on bogs,” says North. “Still, if you’re an average person visiting a bog today and you stay on the marked trail, I am not concerned for your safety.”

#4703. How This Former Weightlifter Lost 80 Pounds After GLP-1s Stopped Working

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

For years, Dana Bichler was a competitive weightlifter. He felt fit and strong competing at 200 to 210 pounds. But wear and tear on his body and aging eventually pushed him to step away from weightlifting. Without the training, he began to gain weight slowly and steadily.

“I tried running, and a few other things, and the weight just crept up,” he told Healthline.

Dieting allowed him to lose about 50 pounds, but he would then regain it. At his heaviest, he weighed close to 300 pounds, which inspired him to visit a weight-loss clinic, where he followed a plan centered on the clinic’s foods.

“It’s a life of deprivation,” Bichler said. “You just can’t live like it.”

About five years ago, he tried a GLP-1 medication and two others a few years later. Each helped him lose weight initially but then stopped working.

“There was really no long-term positive effects or benefits that I saw,” he said.

However, he still takes Mounjaro for blood sugar control because he is prediabetic.

A few years ago, he was diagnosed with fatty liver disease. His condition was tied to obesity and caused scarring on his liver.

Bichler understood the seriousness of the condition as his two younger sisters and his oldest brother also had fatty liver disease. His brother and youngest sister developed cirrhosis, and his brother died after the disease affected other parts of his body.

“I had to do something,” he said. “What I was doing was not working.”

From his home in St. Cloud, Minnesota, Bichler traveled to the University of Minnesota to see a hepatologist, who referred him to a gastroenterologist who had worked with Boston Scientific on the instruments used to perform endoscopic sleeve gastroplasty (ESG).

ESG is a minimally invasive weight loss procedure performed using an FDA-authorized endoscopic suturing system, such as one offered through Boston Scientific’s Endura Weight Loss Solutions.

During ESG, a doctor passes an endoscope through the mouth and uses sutures to fold the stomach into a narrower sleeve. No portion of the stomach is removed, and there are no incisions. The smaller stomach limits how much a person can eat at once.

“Patients typically go home the same day and can return to routine daily activities within two to three days,” Brian Dunkin, MD, chief medical officer at Boston Scientific, told Healthline. “For the right person, that provides another less-invasive option to consider with their healthcare professional.”

While ESG may be a good option for some people who don’t achieve weight loss goals with GLP-1 medications, can’t tolerate them, or don’t want to stay on medication long term, Dunkin said he doesn’t think of it as ESG versus GLP-1 drugs.

“One of the best things GLP-1 medications have done is get more people talking to their doctors about obesity and recognizing it as a chronic disease that deserves treatment,” he said.

Each approach has different benefits, risks, and side effects.

“The goal is finding the right treatment, or combination of treatments, for the right patient at the right time,” said Dunkin.

ESG is indicated for adults with obesity with a BMI between 30 and 50, but Dunkin said BMI is only part of the conversation. ESG may be an option for people who aren’t getting the weight loss results they want, who don’t want to stay on weight loss medication long term, or for whom bariatric surgery may not be appropriate or desired, he added.

“Obesity is a chronic disease that requires long-term care,” said Dunkin. “ESG is one part of that care, which is why I believe so strongly in a multidisciplinary approach. The goal is to look at the whole person and find a care plan they can sustain over time.”

In March 2025, Bichler decided ESG was a good fit for him and received the procedure at Boston Scientific. At the time, he was 67 years old and on Medicare, which pre-approved the procedure.

“I just felt comfortable with it not being invasive, and I really needed to deal with [my weight], so I did,” he said.

When Bichler underwent ESG he weighed somewhere in the 260s. Today, he weighs 178 pounds.

While the procedure went smoothly, he said the following month was difficult. Because bread, pasta, rice, and carbonated drinks were off the table, he had to consume clear liquids, then slowly moved to other liquids, and eventually cream soups.

“I found that extremely difficult,” he said.

What surprised him most was depression. Looking back, he calls it a perfect storm. Working with his weight loss doctor, he had stopped taking his antidepressant about two weeks before the procedure. After surgery, his eating habits changed dramatically, disrupting the social life he’d built around food.

“I was in a pretty deep funk for a while,” he said. “I really was.”

He restarted his antidepressant, and over time, he adjusted to a new way of eating.

“I’ve discovered I like cream soup,” he said. “I still have it for meals.”

Although he’s lost more than 80 pounds, Bichler said the bigger change is how good he feels. He exercises four to five days a week and has more energy and moves more easily than he has in years.

“I haven’t felt this good in 30 years,” Bichler said. “I’m not kidding you.”

He’s able to enjoy things he loves like working on the farm he and his wife own. At the farm, he hunts ducks, turkeys, pheasants, and small game, and runs a trapline, all activities his weight had made nearly impossible for a long time.

“It used to be really hard for me to do because of the physicality of doing some of these things,” he said.

Although he retired from his profession, Bichler said he’s busier than ever. He’s a protodeacon in the Eastern Orthodox Church and also serves as a chaplain for his local police department, a role that has him climbing in and out of squad cars and up and down steps.

“Before I’d be sucking air trying to keep up,” he said.

Most meaningful of all is that he has more energy to give to his family.

“I have a grandson that I can actually do things and be active with now,” Bichler said. “It’s like starting all over. I just feel like a new person.”

#4702. Range Energy shows how its eTrailer saves almost as much as a Tesla Semi

Range Energy, a company working to electrify trucking through the use of a trailer with its own battery and motors, has published an analysis showing how much fleets can save through electrification – and just at the right time, with diesel at record highs.

You may have heard a little something about diesel prices lately, which have just about doubled in less than a year due to Donald Trump’s war of choice in Iran.

Diesel is now at record highs, and it’s devastating fleets and truck drivers and anyone who uses any products that are delivered on trucks (so, everyone). It’s an urgent problem that needs an urgent solution, and solutions are not forthcoming from the responsible entities.

So, fleets have to seek another solution, and Range Energy would like to be the one that provides it.

Range is a startup based in California, founded and staffed by former Tesla employees and others from around the EV industry. It’s building an electrified trailer which we demoed at ACT Expo in 2024 (really, watch it, it’s a very cool demo) which promises to cut fleet fuel use significantly.

It does this by having its own battery and motors inside the trailer, meaning the tractor doesn’t have to work nearly as hard as the trailer can effectively pull its own weight. Even though the tractor still runs on diesel, it uses a whole lot less of it.

This differs from the other popular option for fleets: full electrification. There are a number of electric semi tractors available, and fleets have been moving to install them, getting their depots ready for charging. But Range lets you bring your own tractor, and electrifies the trailer instead.

Range previously published some early findings, showing a 36% reduction in fuel use in a testing scenario. It also did a pilot program with an egg farm in California, which improved the fuel efficiency of the farm’s diesel fleet by 50-70%.

Now Range has published its own white paper showing comparative savings that fleets can achieve with either its own solution, the eTrailer, or Tesla’s solution, the fully electric Tesla Semi. The paper does not cover the various other electric semi tractors available on the market today, just a face-off between Range and Tesla.

The analysis goes through several scenarios, mostly focusing on refrigerated trailer units (“reefers”), which is the first product Range is focusing on.

Trailer electrification is a great idea for reefers, because they usually fill up on volume rather than weight (called “cubing out”), meaning battery weight doesn’t eat into maximum trailer payload. Batteries also offer power to run refrigeration, meaning you don’t need to have a diesel generator on the trailer.

The upshot of the whole thing is that: fleets can save money with the Range eTrailer, and can theoretically save more money with the Tesla Semi, but the numbers are relatively close in the most common scenario, and the Tesla scenarios have a much wider spread depending on what implementation you consider.

For example, if you only use public chargers rather than your own depot, the Tesla Semi will be more costly because energy will be more expensive to your fleet than if you bought it at commercial utility rates. So, even though installing chargers in your depot sounds expensive, it will pencil out better in the end.

The best money savings came from having two Semis share the same charger, but that requires tight timings and overnight driving.

Another important feature Range points out is build time for a project. The nice thing about the eTrailer is it can slot into fleets immediately with little operational change required, whereas the larger charging needs of an electric tractor) tend to require bigger projects to get a depot ready with chargers (but despite the higher upfront costs, you get better long-term savings, since you avoid diesel entirely with an electric tractor).

In the end, Range found that its solution saves a little more money than the Tesla Semi does in most scenarios, but the difference is quite narrow, with each option having its strengths and weaknesses. Both solutions are better than diesel in most scenarios, but not all of them.

You don’t necessarily need to choose between the two, as an electrified trailer can still be used with an electric tractor. It works the same way in either case – using its own motors to take some of the effort off the tractor. This means extended range, for longer hauls with light loads that couldn’t quite make it on the Tesla Semi’s inherent range. And the benefit of being able to run the reefer while disconnected from the tractor or shore power remains as well.

The analysis has plenty of limitations. It has to estimate future diesel costs (it used a number below current prices, but still historically high), didn’t cover financing costs, it doesn’t have real-world data for the Tesla Semi, didn’t cover electrified tractor or trailer options from other companies, can’t analyze individual charging costs site-to-site since each is specific to a utility company, didn’t cover the myriad incentives available in various regions, and most of all it didn’t consider diesel emissions, which are a huge societal cost to everyone that electrification reduces (and full electrification reduces more).

So in the end, every fleet has a different use case, and should run the numbers themselves to see how either solution would fit in. But in the generalized case, it looks like there are plenty of savings available out there, whether through tractor or trailer electrification.

A good idea in theory but there are three trailers for every tractor-cab because trailers spend a lot of time sitting idle. For specific closed-loop customers and routes this can very very helpful but not as a general solution.

You know what can offer relief right now? Importing Class 8 Trucks. China is selling 280,000 heavy duty EV trucks this year. Trade barriers hurt economies.

Unfortunately, given diesel prices are at record highs right now, both of the options in the paper are a little suboptimal. Tesla Semis have been on order for almost ten years now, and Tesla only just claimed it has started production in earnest. And Range is still about a year out from volume production of its eTrailer, which it says will start in late 2027 – so, while an eTrailer will be able to slot into a fleet immediately when it’s available, it’s not available yet, which puts a damper on that potential benefit.

So neither can offer immediate relief, but both offer good options for fleets to plan for the next inevitable oil shock – which is why Range didn’t base its analysis solely on current prices (remember, we just had another shock in 2022, this nonsense happens all the time, maybe it’s time to stop using oil). But, the numbers in the paper for the Tesla Semi can be compared to numbers for other electric tractors already available today, which can in turn be compared to the costs of the eTrailer, for fleets so inclined to make that comparison.

#4701. If You're Driving With a Suspended License, Maybe Don't Do 105 MPH in This Particular Chevy Camaro

The driver was arrested after Arizona police reportedly recorded him traveling 30 mph over the limit, with a license suspended three times over.

If you've already been cited multiple times this year for driving on a suspended license, you shouldn't be behind the wheel. You certainly shouldn't be driving a sixth-generation Chevrolet Camaro with no hood, no front clip, and a massive Hi-Ram intake sticking out of the engine bay. And if you insist on driving that Camaro anyway, you probably shouldn't be doing 105 miles an hour in a 75-mph zone. Well, one Arizona driver allegedly managed to do all three, and his reward was a trip to jail.

According to the Arizona Department of Public Safety (AZDPS), a Highway Patrol State Trooper was on traffic duty on Interstate 10 on Sunday, October 25, when spotted the hard-to-miss Camaro in the left lane allegedly traveling at more than 100 mph. And in a delicious twist, in order to catch up to the speeding car, the police deployed a sixth-generation Camaro of their own.

The trooper pulled the Camaro over and asked the driver if he had a valid driver's license. The driver reportedly responded that he did, but unfortunately, a records check revealed that wasn't exactly true. It turns out the driver apparently had quite a history of license suspensions: according to authorities, his license was suspended in January 2026 for financial responsibility issues, followed by another suspension in March for street racing, and a third in June for failing to appear in court.

When the trooper asked whether he knew his license was suspended, the driver reportedly admitted that he believed it was. (Apparently, that wasn't enough to convince him to stop driving his attention-magnet Camaro.) And this time, it cost him more than just a citation; the driver was arrested on charges of criminal speeding and driving on a suspended license.

If three license suspensions and multiple citations weren't enough to teach this driver a lesson, perhaps time behind bars will do the trick. In the meantime, the winner of this Camaro-versus-Camaro showdown wasn't the one with the massive aftermarket intake; it was the one with the flashing lights.

#4700. Unknown bald eagle spotted on Shadow’s nest

Published Oct 27, 2026 4:18 PM EDT

The bald eagle nest in Big Bear Valley has welcomed a new visitor. On Tuesday, cameras spotted an unknown adult spending time in the nest once shared by Jackie and Shadow.

The new eagle was first seen last week, but returned on Tuesday for about 30 minutes to fiddle with a few sticks and pose in front of the nest cam operated by Friends of Big Bear Valley (FOBBV). A sub-adult eagle has also been spotted on FOBBV’s cameras in recent weeks. Shadow has not been seen by the cameras since October 23. Kaydee, a young adult bald eagle who has been seen arranging sticks and singing with Shadow in the past few months, was last seen on October 21.

It’s not unusual for bald eagles to spend less time in their nests in the fall. Fans often refer to this time as “bald eagle vacation,” where the birds will spend time exploring other parts of the area and sleeping in trees with more cover. Mating season for the Big Bear Valley bald eagles typically starts in December. It’s not yet known if Shadow will return to his nest or mate with a new partner following the death of Jackie on August 10.

Jackie and Shadow were not the original inhabitants of the nest seen on the FOBBV cams. Jackie’s parents, Lucy and Ricky, built the nest during the 2012-2013 nesting season. Shortly after the 2011-2012 nesting season, when Jackie was born and eventually fledged, Lucy and Ricky’s old nest blew away in a strong storm.

The old nest sat at the top of a dead tree. The new nest occupied a nearby, stronger tree about 50 feet away from where Jackie was raised. Lucy and Ricky abandoned the nest in the 2015-2016 season, opting instead to build a new nest nearby. At the beginning of the 2016-2017 nesting season, Lucy and Ricky disappeared from the area. It’s unknown where they went or what happened to them. But that same season, a juvenile female began hanging out at their old pad. Experts later guessed this was Jackie. She used this nest, first with original partner Mr. B and later with Shadow, until her death.

In summer 2026, Shadow continued to tend to the nest with the pair’s chicks, Sandy and Luna, until they fledged in mid-July. In the months that followed, he continued to visit the nest and eventually allowed Kaydee to also spend time there.

Stay tuned to the FOBBV cameras to see how this bald eagle story continues to unfold. Camera 1 (the main nest cam) is currently running its usual 24/7 streaming schedule, but Camera 2 (the wide angle) is currently being turned off at night to conserve energy.

#4699. Volkswagen gets L3 autonomous driving test permit in China, eyes 2027

Volkswagen Group China now has a permit to test Level 3 autonomous driving on public roads in Hefei, and it says testing is already underway. The permit also covers large-scale driving data collection in the city.

It’s the latest step toward VW’s goal of L3 technology readiness in China by 2027. And the timing is good as the group holds its first China Technology Day in Hefei on Wednesday.

VW says the permit was issued under China’s strictest L3 framework and that its setup meets the country’s latest mandatory safety design standards. It didn’t say which authority issued it, how many vehicles are in the fleet, or which roads they can use.

Hefei makes sense as a base. It’s home to the Volkswagen China Technology Company (VCTC), the group’s largest R&D center outside Germany, and to its Volkswagen Anhui production site.

The software comes from CARIZON, VW’s intelligent driving unit in China, which started as a joint venture between CARIAD and Horizon Robotics. Its driver assistance system is called Hyper Sense 8 (HS8), which VW describes as its first “full-scenario” ADAS.

Behind it is GAIA 2.0, a world model VW built itself. VW says it runs simulation equal to 5 million km of safety testing per day, using about 30 million real-road scenario clips, and it wants to get that to 10 million km per day. VW is also developing its own system-on-chip, the C7H, which it says can support up to Level 4.

Ralf Brandstätter, chairman and CEO of Volkswagen Group China, kept the message on safety. He said the group “will never advance technology at the cost of safety” and called the permit an important step on the road to L3 readiness (our translation from Chinese).

This is a road test permit. VW can’t sell L3 cars to customers with it.

China’s MIIT granted the country’s first L3 product approvals in December 2025 to two sedans: a Changan model capped at 50 km/h on designated Chongqing expressways, and a BAIC Arcfox model capped at 80 km/h on three Beijing routes. GAC’s Hyptec and XPeng already hold L3 road test permits too. So VW isn’t leading here. It’s catching up to Chinese brands on their home turf.

In July, VW, CARIZON, and Horizon Robotics said they would deepen their partnership, giving CARIZON “white-box” access to Horizon’s AI foundation model, and targeted the start of L3 deliveries in the second half of 2027. VW’s L2++ system is rolling out on seven new NEV models from its Chinese joint ventures this year.

VW also leans on XPeng in China. It bought a roughly 5% stake in XPeng in 2023 and co-developed its China zonal electrical architecture, CEA, with the startup.

Outside China, the only Western automaker with a certified L3 system on sale is Mercedes-Benz, whose Drive Pilot works on approved highways in Germany and in California and Nevada. Mercedes also got approval to test Level 4 driving in Beijing back in 2024. Tesla’s FSD remains a Level 2 system everywhere it’s sold, China included.

L3 is where liability moves. When the system is engaged, the automaker is responsible for the driving, not the person in the seat. That’s why so few companies have shipped it, and why the ones that have keep it on a short leash: specific roads, low speeds, mostly traffic jams.

China has been serious about building a framework for automakers to bring this techonology to market, and through it, we are seeing who is interested in this version of autonomy.

Not everyone is. Many automakers, including Tesla, have been talking about “skipping” level 3 and going straight to level 4.
