#4666. Lectric launches XP Lite3 e-bike, the new best low-cost model in the US

Lectric eBikes, the largest electric bike company in the US by just about any metric you can measure, has just unveiled its latest model: the Lectric XP Lite3. And with a starting price of just $799, the new lightweight folding electric bike is continuing the company’s tradition of packing surprisingly impressive features into remarkably affordable e-bikes.

The XP Lite2 had been widely considered the best bang-for-your-buck option in the ultra-budget category, offering an affordable yet punchy Class 2 e-bike for a song, despite still coming from a reputable US-based company with strong reputation for warranty and support.

Now, the third-generation model builds on what has become one of the most successful budget e-bike platforms in the country, bringing a long list of upgrades designed to make the bike easier to ride, fold, transport, and live with.

And perhaps most importantly, Lectric has managed to keep that familiar $799 starting price that debuted on the original XP Lite1 all the way back in 2022.

The new Lectric XP Lite3 weighs just 49 lb (22.2 kg), making it one of the lighter options in Lectric’s extensive lineup of folding electric bikes. That’s still no featherweight, partly due to Lectric’s insistence on not neutering the bike’s performance, but it’s still a solid 10-20 lb lighter than the average direct-to-consumer e-bike these days.

The bike retains the compact folding design that made its predecessors popular with everyone from college students to RV owners, but introduces a redesigned frame with improved ergonomics and a reinforced folding latch borrowed from the company’s flagship XP4 model.

New quick-release pedals further reduce the bike’s storage footprint, making it easier to squeeze into a car trunk, apartment closet, or RV storage compartment.

Despite its compact dimensions, the XP Lite3 can support a maximum payload of 275 lb (125 kg) and accommodates riders ranging from 4’8” to 6’2”.

The bike reaches speeds of up to 20 mph (32 km/h) and offers up to 40 miles (64 km) or 80 miles (128 km) of range in Eco mode, though expect significantly less range when using higher-power pedal assist or throttle-only riding. The range discrepancy comes from two different battery offerings. The base model features a 374 Wh battery, while the long-range version has nearly twice the capacity at 672 Wh.

Power comes from Lectric’s Stealth M24 motor, which is rated at 300W continuous but over 800 peak watts. The motor combines with Lectric’s pedal assist selector to offer five levels of pedal assist that are personalizable, letting riders dial in exactly how much boost they’d like on their ride. Riders also get a twist throttle, a more comfortable style of throttle enabled by the lack of shifters crowding the bars on this single-speed e-bike.

Several other upgrades help the XP Lite3 punch above its weight class, including integrated rear turn signals, a bright 3.5-inch full-color display brought over from other recently launched models in the Lectric lineup, and a redesigned LevelUp Lite rear rack with new mounting possibilities.

Stopping power comes from Star Union 602 hydraulic disc brakes with thicker 2.3 mm rotors, another welcome feature on a bike at this price point.

Lectric is also offering a Gates Carbon Belt Drive version of the XP Lite3, giving riders a cleaner, quieter, and virtually maintenance-free alternative to a traditional chain drivetrain. That Gates belt drive model fetches a $100 premium, but is likely worth it for those who value the cleaner, maintenance-free alternative that is likely to outlast the bike itself.

The chain-drive version comes in Arctic White, Blue Mist, Matte Grey, and Matte Lavender, while the belt-drive model is offered in JW Black and Ballerina Pink.

It’s difficult to overstate just how much Lectric has changed the American electric bicycle industry.

The Phoenix, Arizona-based company has grown into the country’s largest e-bike brand by both sales volume and the total number of e-bikes on the road. In doing so, it has become one of the most recognizable names in affordable electric transportation.

But Lectric didn’t get there by simply building cheap electric bikes.

Instead, the company helped revolutionize what consumers should expect from a budget-friendly e-bike, combining capable hardware, practical designs, and aggressive pricing with something that has historically been missing from much of the low-cost e-bike market: a real American company standing behind the product.

While countless inexpensive e-bikes sold online come from little-known overseas brands with questionable long-term support, Lectric has built its reputation around US-based customer service, accessible replacement parts, and a company that riders can actually reach when something goes wrong.

That’s a big part of what has made the XP Lite series so important.

Since its introduction, the XP Lite series has arguably set the standard for what an entry-level electric bike should be. It isn’t necessarily the most powerful, fastest, or fanciest e-bike on the road, but it delivers the essentials at a price that opens electric cycling to an entirely new audience.

And importantly, it does so without requiring riders to gamble on an unknown brand.

The XP Lite3 continues that formula, adding features like hydraulic disc brakes, integrated turn signals, and a color display that would have been difficult to imagine on a $799 e-bike just a few years ago.

I’ve been following Lectric since the company’s earliest days, and it’s been fascinating to watch how the brand has consistently raised the bar for affordable electric bikes. I rode one of Lectric’s first 10 bikes off their nascent production line all the way back in 2019, and I think they’d agree that few people outside the company know the brand better than I do. So I can say that, without a doubt, this is one of the company’s most important launches to date because of how it revolutionizes how much bike someone can get without stretching their budget farther than they have to. And at a time when inflation is still rising unchecked and fuel prices are through the roof, this is what the industry needs more than ever.

Keep in mind that the $799 price tag for the XP Lite3 announced today is the same price that the original XP Lite carried back in 2022, despite that value ballooning to $939 in 2026 dollars due to rising inflation.

What impresses me most isn’t necessarily any single feature on the new XP Lite3. It’s the combination of all those features at a price that remains accessible to so many riders.

Hydraulic brakes, a color display, integrated turn signals, a refined folding mechanism, and even the option for a Gates belt drive? That’s quite a lot of bike for the money. And remember, the performance is still there. This is still a 48V e-bike with a legit 20 mph (32 km/h) top speed on throttle and pedal assist.

Sure, there are lighter e-bikes out there, and there are certainly more premium models with fancier components. But that’s not really the point of the XP Lite.

The point is to make electric biking accessible without making it feel like a compromise at every turn.

And when you consider that you’re getting all of this from the biggest e-bike company in the country, complete with US-based support and a proven track record, it’s hard to argue with the value proposition.

The original XP Lite helped establish what a good affordable electric bike could be. The XP Lite3 looks ready to move that benchmark forward once again.

And on a personal note, not only do I want my own Lectric XP Lite3 now, but I think my wife’s new e-bike will soon be an XP Lite3 in Ballerina Pink with a Gates belt drive. Remember, “Happy wife, happy life!”

#4665. Permanent Daylight Saving Time is dangerous for kids, new research says

Published Oct 29, 2026 11:00 AM EDT

Daylight Saving Time (DST) has always been contentious. In the United States, the debate resurfaces almost as regularly as everyone shifts their clocks backwards in the fall and forward in the spring. Earlier this year, the U.S. House of Representatives even passed a bill called the “Sunshine Protection Act” to make DST permanent. However, the legislation hasn’t progressed much further since July, and we are mere days away from falling back.

That’s for the best, according to a team of biologists at the University of Washington, Seattle (UW). In a study published today in the journal Current Biology, researchers contend a permanent DST would needlessly endanger countless children around the country during their morning school commutes.

“Permanent DST would move the school day earlier relative to the sun without changing a single bell schedule, putting millions of children on streets and at bus stops in the dark for weeks or months every year,” said study co-author and UW chronobiologist Horacio de la Iglesia.

De la Iglesia and his colleagues explained that while most DST chatter centers on how much light is available during evening hours, it ignores the early morning consequences. Most children in the U.S. return home from school before sundown with or without DST, but a permanent shift could make predawn commutes a regular occurrence around the country. According to de la Iglesia’s team, authors of the Sunrise Protection Act didn’t factor in these issues before the school day when crafting their bill.

To investigate, researchers the team examined school start times in 14 states with a hypothetical permanent DST, then compared them to local sunrise times. They calculated roughly 356 million additional trips to school before sunrise. When expanded to the entire country, the authors estimate over two billion predawn school trips. From there, the study authors reviewed available traffic data to determine that dark mornings dramatically increase the chances of pedestrian collisions. Fatal instances involving individuals ages 5 to 18 are more likely during dark hours, too.

The ramifications aren’t concentrated in any single region of the country, either. Northern and southern states would all be affected, although Georgia would likely experience the most dark morning commutes in the nation. That said, permanent DST would negatively affect more children based on socio-economic lines.

“The burden of permanent DST is likely greatest for children who walk, wait for buses, or arrive early for school breakfast programs, which disproportionately serve lower-income families,” added UW biologist and study co-author Guadalupe Rodríguez Ferrante.

If the U.S. ever did pass a similar law, Ferrante and de la Iglesia argued that it should be for a permanent standard time (ST). That switch would reduce the current number of dark school mornings by half. A permanent ST is also more aligned with the biological and social clocks of children and adolescents.

“No clock policy adds a single minute of daylight. It only changes when that daylight is available,” said de la Iglesia. “Permanent DST moves an hour of light out of the morning, when children travel to school, and into the evening.”

But if all that somehow weren’t enough, the study’s authors contend that historical precedent should ensure the “Sunshine Protection Act” never sees the light of day, so to speak.

“The U.S. has tried this before,” said Ferrante, referring to a year-round DST that went into effect in January 1974.

The shift didn’t even last a year—in large part due to worries about children heading to school.

#4664. Ford’s new sub-$30K electric truck can power your home for a lot less

Ford wants to make powering your home with an EV a lot cheaper. Its upcoming sub-$30,000 Fathom electric truck will feature a new bidirectional charging system that ditches the need for an expensive external inverter.

Arriving in 2027, the Fathom will be the first EV from a US automaker priced below $30,000 that can deliver more than 10 kW of AC power to a home without a separate wall-mounted inverter.

And Ford says it’s cutting the cost of the other equipment needed for home backup power, too.

EV batteries store electricity as direct current (DC), but our homes use alternating current (AC). To send power from an EV battery into a house, traditionally, that meant installing a pricey external inverter.

Ford has come up with a different approach for its new Universal EV Platform, which will underpin the Fathom.

After acquiring startup Auto Motive Power in 2023, Ford redesigned its bidirectional charging system from the ground up. Instead of relying on a separate wall-mounted inverter, it built one directly into the truck’s E-box, one of the vehicle’s five main modules.

Fewer parts mean lower costs, and Ford says the savings will extend to the home charging equipment, too.

Fathom owners will have two ways to use the truck’s battery to power their homes.

Home Power Management will let owners charge their truck when electricity rates are low, then use that stored power at home when rates are higher. That could mean real savings for households on time-of-use electricity plans. They’ll need Ford’s new Home Power Station, which the company expects to cost about half as much as its first-generation bidirectional charger.

Home Backup Power will let the truck keep the lights on during an outage. For that, owners will need both the Home Power Station and Ford’s Home Backup Panel. Ford says the backup hardware should cost at least 60% less than its first-generation equipment.

Ford hasn’t released prices for either piece of hardware, so we don’t yet know what a complete home installation will cost.

But pairing a sub-$30,000 electric truck with substantially cheaper home power equipment could make bidirectional charging a lot more appealing.

Making the hardware cheaper is one thing. Making sure utilities can handle thousands of EVs that send electricity back into homes and potentially the grid is another.

Ford formed a working group in July with American Electric Power, BC Hydro, Consumers Energy, Exelon, and Pacific Gas and Electric. They’re working on making it easier for customers to connect bidirectional EVs before the Fathom arrives next year.

For example, someone using their truck solely for home backup power during an outage shouldn’t have to go through the same approval process as someone sending electricity to the grid.

The group is also looking at how to update utility procedures to accommodate newer bidirectional charging standards and make it easier for EV owners to participate in virtual power plants (VPPs). In other words, the batteries in parked EVs could become a useful source of electricity when the grid needs it most.

Ford says the Fathom’s system is designed to meet applicable UL 1741 requirements and IEEE 1547 interconnection standards. It also uses SAE J3068 communications technology, which Ford says helps reduce charger costs.

The idea is to get the technical requirements and utility processes sorted out before affordable bidirectional EVs start arriving in much larger numbers.

Affordable EVs already offer some form of bidirectional power. Two of the cheapest electric cars in the US, the Chevy Bolt and Nissan Leaf, are both available for under $30,000.

The Bolt supports vehicle-to-home (V2H) power through GM Energy equipment, while the Leaf offers vehicle-to-load (V2L) capability through an external device plugged into its charging port.

Ford’s system takes things much further. It can deliver more than 10 kW of AC power to a home without an expensive external inverter, and Ford says the rest of the equipment will cost considerably less, too.

That’s a pretty compelling proposition, especially for people who live in areas prone to power outages or have electricity plans with higher peak-hour rates.

When power outages last a while the area still affected shrinks. While a whole county may be out day one, by day 3 it may just be your neighborhood left. At that point you could drive across town and recharge the car and be good to power your house for another few days.

There are still some unknowns. Ford hasn’t announced the final hardware prices, and installation costs will vary. Plus, utility rules need to catch up if EV owners are going to take full advantage of bidirectional charging.

But this seems to be going in the right direction. If automakers can bring costs down and the industry can agree on consistent standards, having an EV that doubles as a home battery could eventually become a normal part of EV ownership rather than an expensive bonus feature.

#4663. Texas Police Are Keeping the Public Safe With a 710-HP Dodge Durango SRT Hellcat

Everything is bigger in Texas—including, it seems, the amount of horsepower needed to serve and protect.

Texas is the biggest state in the lower 48. From its chicken-fried steaks to its Buc-ee's travel centers, the Lone Star State takes advantage of all that space by making everything bigger than you might expect. Now, the Texas Department of Public Safety (DPS) is getting in on the act: The DPS’s North Texas Region recently announced on Facebook that a Dodge Durango SRT Hellcat will be joining its fleet. Because in Texas, a 710-horsepower police SUV is completely reasonable.

The Texas DPS didn't go into much detail about how the Durango SRT Hellcat would be deployed. It simply said: "All that horsepower. One mission: Public Safety." That mission apparently calls for an SUV with a supercharged 6.2-liter V8 under the hood. With a top speed of 180 miles per hour, the Durango SRT Hellcat can cover a lot of ground quickly, and in an emergency, every second counts.

Of course, top speed is only one part of the equation. If the Texas DPS ever finds itself considering a PIT maneuver on a Texas-sized pickup truck, having roughly 5600 pounds of SUV at its disposal might be reassuring. Whether putting an $80,000 Hellcat through that kind of punishment is a good idea is another question entirely.

There is one thing the Texas DPS will need to keep in mind if it intends to use the Durango SRT Hellcat in highway pursuits: range. The EPA rates the supercharged SUV at just 14 miles per gallon combined, and that figure is likely to be far lower when the V-8 is in maximum attack mode. (Our testing saw just 10.7 mpg in the significantly less powerful 2026 Durango R/T 392, for reference.)

Whether this Durango will spend its days chasing bad guys or simply making appearances at community events remains to be seen. (Road & Track has reached out to the Texas DPS for comment, but did not hear back by the time of publication.) But no matter how it is used, it’s certainly going to attract plenty of attention. And while a Hellcat might seem excessive for a police vehicle ... this is Texas we're talking about.

#4662. Extremely chill bear named Paul wins a Dude-approved award

Published Oct 29, 2026 12:09 PM EDT

Like people (and snowflakes), no two bears are alike. Some have their own innovative fishing styles, or “walk on water,” while others will even adopt cubs who are not their own. And a bear named Paul is known for his patience. Paul lives in southeastern Alaska, where he spends his summers catching fish in Anan Creek. He is also the winner of the 2026 Dude abides Award from the United States Forest Service team in Tongass National Forest.

According to the team, Paul exhibits the patience and nonchalance of The Dude, an extremely chill character from the 1998 film The Big Lebowski. Brought to life by Jeff Bridges, The Dude’s catchphrase “The Dude abides” is the final line of the movie, and what inspired this award.

“Paul chose kindness over combat when his fish were stolen,” the team writes. “This bear was seen with a fish in his mouth more frequently than without, and opportunistic rivals with lesser skills in fishing liked to steal his catch.”

Anan Creek is home to one of the largest salmon runs in the world, so defending all of his catches is a waste of energy. As a result, Paul abides, since fishing is more rewarding than fighting.

Paul is known for two thin lines on his chest with a scar on his left ear and won the award for pickiest bear in 2024.

The U.S. Forest Service team at Tongass National Forest are currently doling out the Anan Bear Awards to the 39 bears spotted at the Anan Wildlife Observatory in Tongass National Forest.

The nation’s largest national forest, Tongass covers most of Southeast Alaska, including the capital city of Juneau. The area includes Mendanhall Glacier (a popular destination for Alaskan cruises), numerous hiking trails, eagles, and plenty of bears. One of the hotspots is Anan Creek, home to one of the largest runs of pink salmon in Southeast Alaska.

According to Friends of Anan, 39 known bears feast on the salmon at Anan Creek. The population includes 31 black bears (Ursus americanus) and eight brown bears (Ursus arctos). Like their counterparts further north in Katmai National Park, the bears return annually each summer to eat salmon and teach their young how to fish and survive. And also like the fat bears of Katmai, every bear here has their own habits and quirks.

The U.S. Forest Service tracks and documents every bear and explore.org’s cameras also broadcast live streams of their antics.

#4661. Taking Fish Oil to Boost Brain Health? A 2-Year Study Questions the Benefits

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

A clinical trial found that taking high dose omega-3 supplements for 2 years did not help memory or thinking skills in older adults at increased risk of Alzheimer’s.Researchers at Keck Medicine of USC led the study, which was published in eBioMedicine. Participants took either a daily high dose supplement of omega-3 fatty acid docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) or a placebo.Fish oil is one of the most familiar ways people get omega-3s. However, the supplement in this clinical trial wasn’t made from fish, Hussein Yassine, MD, director of the USC Center for Personalized Brain Health with Keck Medicine of USC and the study’s lead researcher, told Healthline. This article uses the broader term omega-3 supplements.The researchers found that taking supplements raised omega-3 levels in participants’ brains, yet it didn’t change their memory, thinking skills, or brain structure.Dung Trinh, MD, an internist at MemorialCare Medical Group and chief medical officer of Healthy Brain Clinic in Irvine, California, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that the findings challenge the common belief that omega-3 supplements, such as fish oil, can help prevent Alzheimer’s disease or improve memory.Millions of older adults take omega-3 supplements. In a 2017–2018 federal survey, 21.8% of U.S. adults age 60 and older reported taking an omega-3 fatty acid supplement in the past 30 days, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

Getting omega-3s from food or supplements is important since the body cannot make them.

Keck Medicine researchers enrolled 365 adults who did not have dementia, and whose ages ranged from 55 to 80, with an average age of 66.

Subjects obtained little DHA from their diets and had at least one risk factor for dementia. Of the 365 people who enrolled, 225 completed the trial, according to the study. Nearly half (47%) carried APOE4.Participants took either 2,000 milligrams (mg) of DHA or a placebo every day. Neither participants nor researchers knew who received the supplement.

The supplement in the trial contained more than 90% DHA and about 1% EPA, Yassine said.

Researchers found that high dose omega-3 supplements raised DHA levels in the fluid around the brain and spinal cord by 17%.

Both groups in the trial scored about the same on memory and thinking tests. Brain structure appeared the same in both groups.

The supplement also raised omega-3 levels in the blood. Over two years, participants’ omega-3 index, a measure of EPA and DHA in red blood cells, rose from 4.9% to 11%.“That’s a massive increase, but that doesn’t translate into clinical outcomes,” Yassine said.DHA reached the brain equally well in people with and without the gene variant APOE4, which is linked to a higher risk of Alzheimer’s disease, according to the study.Earlier trials couldn’t tell whether DHA failed to reach the brain or reached it without helping, the study’s authors say. This trial answers that open question, since the DHA got there.“This tells us that just because a supplement reaches the brain doesn’t necessarily mean it will improve brain function or prevent cognitive decline,” Trinh said.

The lack of measurable change in memory and thinking may come down to how the body uses omega-3s, according to Yassine.He said it’s “really important to distinguish between omega-3 metabolism and omega-3 supplements.”A supplement can raise omega-3 levels, yet the body may still break them down before they reach the right places. Obesity, smoking, and a lack of exercise can all reduce how much omega-3 gets into the brain, he said.

Some fish and fish oil supplements may offer more than omega-3s. These sources may also include other nutrients such as lutein, vitamin E, and selenium, Yassine said.A supplement can raise the level, but if you don’t change the holistic program, just going and increasing the level by itself may not be sufficient,” he said.Researchers tend to fall into two camps on how to read the results, according to Yassine.

Some see the findings as evidence that supplements don’t work in isolation. Others argue the trial would need a longer follow-up or sicker participants to answer the question.Trinh pointed to the study’s length. “It’s also important to recognize that Alzheimer’s disease develops over decades, so a two-year study may not be long enough to determine whether DHA supplementation has any long-term preventive benefits,” he said.

Fish oil supplements contain two omega-3 fatty acids, eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) and DHA, according to the National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NCCIH).

Foods such as fish and flaxseed also contain omega-3s, according to the National Institutes of Health’s Office of Dietary Supplements (ODS).Research suggests omega-3s may help reduce inflammation, support heart health, and promote childhood growth and development.

Some observational studies link diets high in omega-3s with a lower risk of cognitive decline and dementia.

Researchers say omega-3s may help preserve cognition by supporting brain cells in continuing to function and maintain their membranes, according to the ODS.“Omega-3s are important for the brain, and we and many others have shown that having higher levels of omega-3s is associated with less Alzheimer’s pathology, better cognition, and many other protective outcomes,” Yassine said, in contrast to the trial findings.Trinh agreed. “DHA plays an essential role in maintaining healthy brain cells, and there is evidence that eating fish as part of a healthy dietary pattern may support long-term brain health,” he said.Research on omega-3s and brain health is ongoing, and there is insufficient evidence to draw firm conclusions about their effectiveness.

Some people may still benefit from a supplement, according to Yassine, including:

Some neurologists test omega-3 levels, though the test isn’t standard, Yassine said.People with nutritional deficiencies or certain genetic or metabolic traits may respond differently to omega-3 supplements, and researchers still need to learn who might benefit, Trinh said.

People who already take fish oil or other omega-3 supplements for other reasons, such as high triglycerides, should make those decisions with their healthcare professionals, he said.

Trinh said he tells his patients that “what is good for the heart is generally good for the brain.” He recommended the following healthy habits:

“Overall, this study reminds us that there is no magic pill for preventing Alzheimer’s disease and that maintaining brain health requires a much broader approach,” Trinh said.

#4660. What’s the Best Car Cover for You? Here Are Our Picks

Our car experts choose every product we feature. We may earn money from the links on this page.

For indoor storage, outdoor protection, or a little extra coverage while wrenching in the garage, these are the car covers worth buying.

A car cover is one of the simplest ways to protect a vehicle’s finish, especially when it spends more time parked than on the road. Dust, moisture, UV exposure, bird droppings, and tree sap can all take a toll on paint, even when a car is tucked away in a garage.

For collectors and enthusiasts, that protection can be especially important for seasonal storage, when a classic or weekend toy might sit untouched for months. A well-chosen cover helps keep the finish clean and reduces the work needed to get a car ready for its next drive.

The right cover depends on where and how you plan to use it. A soft, breathable indoor cover is ideal for keeping dust off a collector car, while outdoor models need to stand up to rain, sunlight, and wind without trapping moisture against the paint. Some covers are tailored to specific vehicles for a closer fit, while universal options offer a more affordable solution. There are also temporary covers for garage projects that provide a barrier against dust, overspray, and other messes during detailing, repairs, or restoration work.

I rounded up the best car covers for different vehicles, storage conditions, and budgets, focusing on the features that matter most: material quality, fit, weather resistance, breathability, and ease of use.

💡 Expert Tip: Always start with a clean, dry car before putting on a cover. Dirt and grit trapped between the fabric and paint can act like sandpaper as the cover shifts in the wind, leaving fine scratches and swirl marks. Even the best cover can do more harm than good if it’s used on a dirty car or traps moisture underneath.

For the most part, the CoverSeal looks like any ordinary cover. That is, until you pick it up and realize it weighs far more than you would anticipate. No, it’s not a weighted blanket for your car’s seasonal loneliness. It’s a typical car cover, aside from its patented Ground Seal design.

Rodents can cause chaos in a car’s wiring system, chewing through insulation and potentially causing thousands in damage. CoverSeal covers feature a weighted hem around the base that’s made of powdered sand encased in a malleable plastic tube, to seal the bottom of your vehicle from rodents that might otherwise use the undercarriage as a cozy refuge.

This is CoverSeal’s outdoor model, which uses heavy-duty PVC-coated polyester to protect your vehicle from harmful UV rays and temperatures up to 300 degrees Fahrenheit. It is also offered in an indoor variant, which uses lighter-weight materials and is a bit more affordable.

The affordable EzyShade is one of the most popular covers on the market and an excellent place to begin if you’re in need of a basic outdoor car cover. With 17 sizes, it sits at the intersection of universal and model-specific. I like this compromise between a custom and universal cover that would be less fitted.

The cover itself is made from premium weatherproof materials that have been machine-cut and bond-pressed, resulting in a product that’s up to the task of protecting your vehicle. The underside is soft, and three plastic clasps keep things secure through inclement weather.

Designed with both durability and style in mind, this 18-foot inflatable bubble encases your car in a controlled environment, shielding it from dust, dirt, moisture, and pests. The CarCapsule features a heavy-duty, 10-mil PVC exterior and a powerful, continuous airflow fan that keeps the interior environment stable, preventing condensation and keeping your car in pristine condition.

Aside from this Indoor Showcase model that’s perfect for long-term indoor storage of valuable collector cars, CarCapsule makes indoor and outdoor inflatable bubble enclosures in a number of sizes and styles to suit a variety of vehicles. They’re easy to set up and provide 360-degree protection, ensuring that every inch of your vehicle is safe from scratches, rust, and corrosion.

Seal Skin has made a big space for itself in a crowded segment with a great selection. For example, Seal Skin offers nine sizes just for pickup trucks. Seal Skin also offers a similar variety of covers for cars and SUVs.

This cover is made from high-quality PEVA fabric with a soft cotton lining. An elastic hem helps provide a snug fit, while windproof straps keep the cover taut on windy days. Perhaps my favorite feature is that a cable lock system is included, instantly making this one of the most secure covers you can buy.

If you want even more protection than you can get from Seal Skin’s Amazon storefront, check out the Seal Skin website, where you can find custom-fitted, even higher-quality covers for your specific model.

Covercraft is an industry leader that has been producing some of the most trusted car covers on the market since 1965. The company offers a range of custom-fitted covers for everything from a humble Camry to a Porsche 911 (the cover linked to here) and even more exotic autos. Since these covers are custom-made for each make and model, their fit is far more secure than universal covers. This means less chance of the cover shifting around once it’s installed, which means less chance of your vehicle’s paint being damaged.

The covers use a high-quality fade-resistant material with a HydroMax finish for superior protection against rain, bird droppings, and dust. If you aren’t a 911 owner, check out the Covercraft website and find the model that fits your vehicle.

If you’ve ever been caught in a severe hailstorm, you know that having a basic “all-weather” car cover, while it offers some protection, is like bringing a knife to a gunfight. Warsun covers are designed specifically for protection against hail damage.

The Warsun features a thick oxford-cloth outer layer, a soft and stretchy polyester inner layer, and, most notably, an inflatable PVC airbag liner for impact resistance. Elastic hems offer a tight fit, while zippers at the front and back that allow for adjustment for different-size vehicles. There are also reflective strips for visibility at night. The cover is secured with four straps that have buckle fasteners, and it’s small enough to fit in most standard-size trunks when not in use.

An air pump is included. Warsun notes that this cover is not intended for long-term storage and should be used primarily for severe weather situations.

Sometimes a simple and affordable cover is all you need to keep light rain, dust, and debris off your car. These are great to keep around if you’re a detailer or if the space that your vehicle lives in is shared with a workshop where dust and debris often settle on cars.

These affordable disposable plastic covers come in packs of two, five, or 10 so you can easily double up or replace them as needed. They’re universal but come in three sizes, so be sure to choose the right size for your vehicle.

Before you purchase a car cover, consider what kind of car you’re trying to protect and where it’ll most likely be parked. Covering a collectible in a climate-controlled garage is a far cry from keeping the bird poop off your street-parked beater—and the cost of a car cover always reflects that. Here are some other things to think about.

The old adage “you get what you pay for” really applies to car covers. High-end premium options will cost at least a few hundred dollars—even over $1000 for something like the vaunted CarCapsule—but solutions can be found for under $100 too. It boils down to the type of protection you’re purchasing and how much your vehicle is worth.

A custom-fit car cover is essential if you’re trying to protect a valuable car. Most manufacturers offer fitted covers, so if you’re concerned about protecting an investment—or if you live in a climate where you experience a lot of wind or accumulating sand or snow—buy a car cover that securely fits your vehicle.

Universal car covers are fine for most applications. Don’t be disappointed if the cover blows away in a storm or creatures build a nest in your tailpipe.

Outdoor car covers should be weather-resistant, UV-resistant, and water-resistant. Indoor covers are typically made from softer materials to prevent dust accumulation and minor dings.

Ensure the cover is waterproof or water-resistant for outdoor use to protect against rain and snow. Even for indoor use, a quality cover should protect against things like humidity and garage-roof leaks.

A good cover should offer UV protection to shield your finish, dashboard, and interior from fading or cracking due to sun exposure.

Consider covers with thermal protection if you live in areas with extreme temperatures. Some covers are designed to reflect heat to keep the vehicle cooler.

Higher-quality materials are typically more durable and provide better protection. Check the cover’s thickness and overall construction. Aside from considering quality, the type of material is just as important to keep in mind. Some common materials include:

Some car covers use elastic to seal around a vehicle. These will be the most affordable, but after a while, elastic stretches beyond its usefulness. Some covers use straps that tie or connect with fasteners such as buckles, snaps, and hook-and-loop strips. These covers cost more but should provide extra security, and they’ll last longer. Some feature weighted hems to seal around the base of your vehicle.

For outdoor use, look for covers with adjustable straps or buckles to secure the cover and prevent it from blowing away. To deter theft, some covers come with lock and cable systems.

A well-made car cover with a soft inner lining and a good fit should not scratch your paint. Ensure the cover is clean and free from debris before putting it on your car.

Many car covers are designed to accommodate accessories, but it’s important to choose a cover that fits your specific vehicle setup. Look for covers with adjustable straps or custom fits if you have modifications.

Custom-fit covers are tailored specifically to the dimensions of your vehicle for a snug fit. Universal-fit covers, on the other hand, are designed to fit a range of vehicle sizes and shapes, which might not offer as precise a fit.

Yes, a car cover can trap moisture. It can’t create rust by itself, but it can keep metal damp long enough for corrosion to take hold. Whether a car cover contributes to rust depends on whether it traps moisture against the car for a long time—especially if the car is covered wet, the cover isn’t breathable, or road salt and grime are left on the surface. To lessen the risk, cover a clean, dry car with a well-fitted, breathable cover, and let the cover dry before storing it.

#4659. Rare glob-eyed fish spotted in ocean’s twilight zone

Published Oct 29, 2026 2:01 PM EDT

Few deep-sea species will cause an entire research vessel’s crew to rush into the control room to catch a glimpse—but the barreleye fish (Macropinna microstoma) is one of them. During the Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute’s (MBARI) recent eight-day Diving Deep for Delicate Drifters expedition, oceanographers aboard the David Packard were reunited with one of these rare, surreal creatures for the first time in nearly five years. This time, they successfully recorded the ethereal fish using a high-resolution 4K camera attached to Doc Ricketts, the ship’s remotely operated vehicle (ROV).

“Seeing a barreleye fish is a rare treat,” Steven Haddock, a MBARI senior scientist, said in the institute’s announcement. “Crew from across the ship joined the science team in the control room, mesmerized by this remarkable animal.”

M. microstoma swims through the ocean’s twilight zone, a dim region around 2,000 feet deep in the water column. “Swims” may be a bit generous, however. The barreleye fish spends most of its time drifting in place, while using its large fins to maintain stability. Acute vision is pointless in the near-dark water, so M. microstoma evolved a truly unique set of eyes. The tubular organs roll back far enough to gaze upwards through transparent tissue in its head to hunt for prey. Subtle shadows alert the fish to a target, at which point its eyes rotate forward so it can pursue the potential meal.

Biologists are also fascinated by M. microstoma eyes’ green lenses, which resemble those of the strawberry squid (Histioteuthis heteropsis). Researchers theorize the pigment allows the fish to spot bioluminescence, giving it an additional tool to maneuver through the murky depths.

MBARI marine biologists have conducted around 7,000 ROV dives over almost 40 years of ocean surveys. In the process, they’ve amassed more than 41,000 hours of video footage.. Researchers have only spotted 11 barreleye fish in all that time, and their most recent encounter occurred in 2021.

“[The barreleye fish] reminds us of the surprising ways that animals have adapted to thrive in the ocean’s midwater,” added Haddock. “So many of them survive by looking for subtle optical cues…pitting bioluminescent camouflage against increasingly sophisticated visual capabilities.”

#4658. MIT develops robot that slithers through intestines like a snake

Published Oct 29, 2026 3:10 PM EDT

Worms are usually the last thing someone wants in their gut. Just ask this unfortunate Alaskan bear recently spotted with several multi-foot long tapeworms hanging out of its butt. However, a  new type of gut-crawling worm being designed by engineers at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), may actually be here to help.

Their soft robot, called BIOSENTER, is designed to autonomously inch through the crowded, cramped, and coiled small intestine, contracting and extending its body much like an earthworm or snake. It does that by alternately pumping air through four inflatable chambers on either side of its hollow body. Once inside, the wiggly worm-bot can snap photos, administer drugs, and even take small biopsy samples. It can also slither into the intestine via a person’s mouth or rear-end all by itself.

Horrifying as all of this might sound, the team behind it says the robot could offer a faster, less labor-intensive alternative to double-balloon enteroscopy, the current standard for examining  the small intestine. And with intestinal diseases and cancers on the rise, any methods to detect issues early could have potentially life-saving results. The team published details about the robot this week in the journal Science Robotics.

The small intestine is a particularly challenging place to run diagnoses. Though it can measure 20 feet long, it’s tightly coiled up in a cramped part of the abdomen. It is also hemmed in by the stomach and colon, which can make it difficult to reach.  But bleeding, lessons, and blockages can develop in the small intestine which can lead to big problems if left untreated. Currently, the most common way to examine the organ is double-balloon enteroscopy. Healthcare workers repeatedly inflate and deflate two balloons to work a scope through the digestive tract. The method works, but it’s slow and requires constant hands-on attention.

“The fundamental challenge that we’re trying to overcome is how to evaluate that 20-to-25-foot segment of the small intestine in a way that can be more automated,” Giovanni Traverso, an MIT mechanical engineer and  study-co-author, said in a statement.

The team turned to nature for a solution: snakes. These scaly reptiles move by alternating contracting muscles on either side of their body. Aside from offering protection, their scaly bodies also give them extra traction as they slither. The MIT researchers looked at this natural byproduct of evolution and saw a design that could work well in the narrow, slippery corridors of the human GI tract.

With the snake inspiration in mind, the team built a soft, rubbery robot with a hollow body. Its worm-like frame measures about 3.7 inches in length with a half inch diameter. These dimensions make it compact enough to travel through the small intestine, as well as other narrow passages in the body, like the esophagus. BIOSENTER has four inflatable chambers arranged along either side of its tubular body.  These chambers inflate and deflate in alternating combinations, which is how it moves forewarn and bends to change directions. Keeping with the snake theme, the robot’s exterior is fitted with a textured, scale-like coating that improves its traction.

Additionally, the worm has expandable sections built in its head and tail inspired by a type of Japanese origami called kirigami, that uses cuts as well as folds. These inflatable segments alternately grip and release the intestinal wall, anchoring the robot so it can pull itself forward. BIOSENTER’s hollowed out body houses a variety of tools: cameras for imaging, a sprayer for drug delivery, and tiny clippers to take tissue samples. The entire thing is tethered to an external system via cable. Though it’s meant to move mostly autonomously, healthcare workers can also control BIOSENTER through a handheld device reminiscent of an Xbox controller.

“By using kirigami sleeves to enhance surface friction, the robot can generate localized tissue engagement traction for locomotion without relying on excessive stretching of the delicate small intestinal tissue,” added MIT graduate student Ahmad Mujtaba Jebran..

The team tested the robot on several sedated,  living pigs, because their GI tract anatomy resembles the kind humans have. During testing, BIOSENTER navigated the pigs’ intestines for 11 minutes, capturing real-time images, collecting small tissue biopsies, and delivering fluid to specific locations.

BIOSENTER notably isn’t the first gut-crawling robot. In 2021, a team from the University of Macau in China designed a prototype robot inspired by an African spider that moves using a cartwheel motion. In that case, the robot is injected via a vitamin sized capsule and traverses the GI tract (including the small intestine) via a magnetic field. Rather unglamorously, the spider bot is expelled by pooping.

#4656. Sir Patrick Stewart Dies at 86 After Battle With Alzheimer's, Lewy Body Dementia

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Sir Patrick Stewart, best-known for portraying Captain Jean-Luc Picard in “Star Trek” and Professor Charles Xavier in the “X-Men” film franchise, has died. He was 86.

The legendary actor and thespian passed away on October 28 after a “brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s Disease and Lewy Body Dementia,” according to his longtime spokesperson, Kelly Bush Novak, in a statement to The Hollywood Reporter.

He died peacefully at his home in Los Angeles, where he was receiving care from his wife, Sunny Ozell.

“He has been held in the warm embrace of family and friends, surrounded by live music, prayer, tears, laughter and the kind of profound emotion that only he could inspire after a lifetime of devotion to us all,” Bush Novak wrote in the statement. “We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace.”

Stewart’s acting career spanned more than six decades across theater, television, and film.

A longtime member of the Royal Shakespeare Company, he rose to international fame in 1987 with “Star Trek: The Next Generation” and later became known for his portrayal of Professor Charles Xavier in the 2000 film “X-Men” and its numerous sequels.

He was knighted by Queen Elizabeth II in 2010 for his contributions to drama.

Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia are two progressive neurological conditions that can affect memory, thinking, behavior, and a person’s ability to perform everyday activities.

According to the National Institute on Aging (NIA), both conditions can cause dementia, a term used to describe a decline in cognitive abilities severe enough to interfere with daily life.

Alzheimer’s disease is the most common cause of dementia. The condition is associated with abnormal buildups of proteins called amyloid and tau in the brain, which disrupt communication between nerve cells and contribute to their damage.

The NIA states that memory problems are often among the earliest symptoms of Alzheimer’s. As the disease progresses, people may experience increasing difficulty with language, reasoning, decision making, and recognizing familiar people.

Lewy body dementia, meanwhile, is associated with abnormal deposits of a protein called alpha-synuclein in the brain. These deposits, known as Lewy bodies, affect brain chemicals involved in thinking, movement, mood, and sleep, according to the NIA.

People with Lewy body dementia may experience changes in attention and alertness, visual hallucinations, muscle stiffness, difficulty walking, and sleep disturbances.

According to the Alzheimer’s Association, the two conditions may co-occur, and their overlapping symptoms may make diagnosis more challenging.

Currently, neither condition has a cure, but treatments are available to help manage symptoms. Certain medications can also slow cognitive decline in some people with early Alzheimer’s disease.

#4655. Gamma-ray burst is one of the brightest in decades

Published Oct 29, 2026 4:15 PM EDT

A gamma-ray burst (GRB) that has confounded astronomers is one of the brightest cosmic light shows in the past 20 years. Although the cosmic explosion first appeared inexplicably weak, researchers now believe it actually shot about one billion years’ worth of solar energy into the cosmos through a beam no thicker than a pencil.

“We see hundreds of GRBs every year, but the oddballs are the most informative ones,” said Roberto Ricci, a radioastronomer at Italy’s National Institute of Astrophysics.

Ricci and his colleague’s findings are detailed in a study recently published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters. On March 10, NASA’s Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope observed a burst later classified as GRB 260310A. Gamma-ray bursts most frequently occur in the aftermath of a massive star’s collapse. When this happens, powerful jets of matter launch into space close to the speed of light. These jets collide with cosmic gas, which generates afterglows seen across visible light, radio waves, and X-rays.

While GRB 260310A’s flash of light lasted less than one minute, astronomers noted it seemed to produce strangely little energy. This changed within only a few hours, as GRB 260310A’s afterglow brightened so much that it briefly outshone its host galaxy. A few weeks later, the GRB’s X-ray emissions brightened again and then remained observable for months.

“At first, I thought another X-ray source was contaminating our observations. But the brightening really came from the afterglow,” recalled study co-author and astronomer Yu-Han Yang.

Further observations using an international array of observatories and telescopes later confirmed a supernova had indeed prompted a GRB. Early signs indicated that its jet was pointed away from Earth, but while the gamma-ray readings were comparatively basic, both its visible and X-ray measurements ranked among the top one percent in brightness. GRB 260310A also fell within the top five percent for recorded radio brightness. After reviewing the data, astronomers finally realized what was happening.

“We looked at it from a side angle,” explained Yang. “As the jet slowed down, its light became visible over a wider range of angles, allowing us to probe the jet’s shape, from its outer edges toward its inner core.”

Yang compared most GRB observations to looking directly at a flashlight. Although the light is brightest from that perspective, the beam may appear dimmer if it is viewed from further away. Most GRB modeling is calibrated from events detected from a direct vantage point, but GRB 260310A was different.

“This burst gave us a chance to look beyond that glare,” said Yang.

Astronomers theorize that GRB 260310A may have originated from a jet featuring a very narrow, energized core encompassed by wider, slower outflows. If true, the early afterglow hypothetically traces back to the jet’s wings, while the brightening X-ray phase came from the thin core.

Although it took a moment to decipher, GRB 260310A offers a rarely seen window into a gamma-ray burst. Such opportunities are rare, but the team hopes to find more in the near future using even more powerful tools like the recently completed Vera Rubin Observatory.

“We could explain individual features of this burst, but fitting them all into the same picture proved much harder,” added Ricci.

#4654. Ford’s Off-Road Models and Trims Make Up Nearly a Quarter of the Carmaker’s U.S. Sales So Far This Year

Our car experts choose every product we feature. We may earn money from the links on this page.

Bronco, Raptor, Tremor, and FX4 models made up 24 percent of Ford sales through September, with higher margins adding to their appeal.

It's no secret that off-road trims are becoming more and more popular. Despite the data that suggests that very few people ever really use all that capability, the vehicles often look more attractive to buyers; and a little more ground clearance, chunkier tires, and a name that sounds vaguely adventurous give automakers the license to charge more, too. Ford's latest sales results offer a concrete explanation for why automakers keep going back to that well: buyers keep showing up.

In its third-quarter earnings recap, Ford chief financial officer Sherry House said higher-margin off-road vehicles now account for about a quarter of the company's U.S. sales. She also credited a richer product mix, including Tremor and other off-road trims, with helping Ford increase adjusted earnings despite lower revenue. To be specific, the brand generated $49.5 billion in revenue during the quarter.

That's actually down 2 percent year over year, as adjusted earnings before interest and taxes climbed 3 percent to $2.7 billion. Cost controls helped too, so the credit doesn't all belong to skid plates. Still, Ford clearly likes what those vehicles do for its bottom line.

Its more detailed sales report demonstrates why. Through September, its off-road performance lineup accounted for 364,141 sales, or 24 percent of the company total. That share rose 3.8 percentage points from a year earlier, while volume increased 8.4 percent. Importantly, the brand's definition of "off-road performance" is somewhat broad; it includes Raptor, Tremor, and FX4 packages, across which is a wide swath of hardware, capability, and prices.

And demand still seems to be growing. Raptor sales increased 4.6 percent through September, while Tremor sales jumped 122 percent. The Bronco itself posted record third-quarter sales of 38,020 vehicles. That gives Ford, and automakers with similar offerings, a clear reason to continue leaning into this trend.

The Raptor lineup also highlights a key reason why automakers are keen on the trend: the margins are great. Advertised starting MSRPs as of this story’s publication are $59,860 for the Ranger Raptor, $78,815 for the F-150 Raptor, and $82,685 for the Bronco Raptor. Even the least expensive starts well above the $50,562 industry average transaction price Kelley Blue Book reported for September.

#4653. BYD names its ultra-luxury EV, and it could be a game changer next week

BYD’s new flagship EV will be its largest and most luxurious electric sedan yet, potentially debuting two firsts for the company next week: Rolls-Royce-style coach doors and solid-state batteries.

BYD is better known for its low-cost electric cars, like the Seagull, a little hatchback that sells for under $10,000 in China.

The Chinese auto giant has greatly expanded its portfolio over the past few months and years. BYD now offers everything from entry-level EVs to three-row flagship SUVs, pickup trucks, electric supercars, and just about everything in between.

BYD has three sub-brands: Denza, FangChengBao, and Yangwang. It also has two main families under the BYD brand: the Dynasty and Ocean series.

Yangwang sits at the top of BYD’s brand hierarchy and showcases its latest breakthrough technologies.

Previously, Yangwang vehicles debuted on BYD’s quad-motor e4 platform, delivering a whopping 1,300 horsepower and featuring its DiSus-X intelligent body control system, which enables the vehicle to “dance,” jump, and drive on three wheels.

For its next model, BYD is pushing further into the elite segment to take on ultra-luxury brands like Rolls-Royce, Bentley, and Mercedes-Maybach.

BYD revealed the name of its flagship ultra-luxury EV for the first time on Tuesday: the Yangwang Altior, along with a new teaser of the partially uncovered executive sedan.

Coming soon#YANGWANG #YANGWANGALTIOR pic.twitter.com/kFnu6X6csq

Yangwang general manager Hu Xiaoqing said the name was chosen as an independent Chinese-English naming scheme. In China, it goes by DingYao. The “Ding” symbolizes stability and endurance, while “Yao” signifies radiant brilliance, or shining brightly like a star in the sky.

The English name Altior comes from Latin for “higher,” representing Yangwang’s relentless pursuit of ever-greater heights.

The new teaser comes after Hu revealed several images of the new Yangwang executive sedan testing for the first time last month.

Although it was disguised, it appeared to be about the same shape and size as the Mercedes-Benz Maybach S-Class or Rolls-Royce Phantom. Local reports indicate it will be around 5,500 mm (216″) long.

HU confirmed for the first time last week that the global launch of the new flagship sedan will take place in the UAE, not in BYD’s home market of China.

BYD has not yet revealed a specific launch date, but the Yangwang sedan could make its first appearance as early as next week. According to CarNewsChina, citing “sources familiar with the project,” BYD is aiming to reveal the new flagship model in Dubai, UAE, around November 5.

Zheng Yu, Yangwang’s executive general manager, said the new model will feature “unprecedented disruptive technology,” but didn’t reveal specifics.

Although details are still limited, the ultra-luxury sedan was shown at BYD’s Flash Charging station, suggesting it will support megawatt flash charging.

It also features rear-hinged coach doors, a first for BYD. The flagship EV will reportedly be the first to feature BYD’s solid-state batteries.

BYD executive vice president Stella Li said during an interview with Carwow.es last month that the company’s first vehicle to use solid-state batteries will debut in 2027.

Li said BYD is “in the leading position” in solid-state battery technology and its commercialization, and the company plans to prove it next year.

BYD’s battery unit, FinDreams, plans to begin production of sulfide-based all-solid-state batteries in 2027. It will initially be produced in limited batches, then scale to mass production closer to the end of the decade.

The part about solid state batteries got my attention. I'm looking forward to learning more about how they perform!

While BYD has yet to confirm it, introducing the new battery tech in a flagship model would make sense.

The executive sedan is expected to debut around November 5. Prices are rumored to start in the 2 million yuan range, or about $300,000.

Yangwang’s current electric sedan, the U7, starts at 658,000 yuan ($98,000). The brand also sells the U8 (and U8L), a plug-in hybrid luxury off-road SUV, and the U9, a fully electric super-coupe.

The extended U8L is Yangwang’s highest-priced mass-produced vehicle, starting at 1.45 million yuan ($217,000).

Are candy companies changing their recipes or do we just taste things differently now? Ask Us Anything answers your most outlandish, mind-burning questions—from the everyday things you’ve always wondered to the bizarre things you never thought to ask. #4651. The Vatican Is Celebrating Nearly 100 Years of Popemobiles With a Very Special Car Collection

Our car experts choose every product we feature. We may earn money from the links on this page.

The Pope has been riding in Mercedes-Benz vehicles since 1930, and now, some of His Holiness’s most famous rides are getting their own exhibition.

Pebble Beach, Goodwood, and Amelia Island are all great places to see some of the most historically significant Mercedes-Benz vehicles ever made. Now, however, you can add the Vatican to that list. The newest exhibition at The Vatican Museums is called “A Century of the Popemobile,” and it celebrates nearly 100 years of Mercedes-Benz vehicles built for the Pope.

The new exhibition kicks off roughly a year and a half into the papacy of Pope Leo XIV, the first American-born pope (and a man who is reportedly a big car fan, according to the Associated Press). Leo, who was recently gifted a bespoke 2026 Ford Explorer by Ford CEO Jim Farley and checked out the new Ferrari Luce after its reveal, reportedly met with Mercedes-Benz executives to thank them for their long-term partnership with the Catholic Church’s highest office.

According to a report by Vatican News, there will be eight historic Mercedes-Benz vehicles on display. The oldest car in the exhibit is a Mercedes-Benz Nürburg 460 Pullman limousine that was delivered to Pope Pius XI in 1930. Its luxurious interior featured silk brocade upholstery, elaborate wood and metal trim, and a decorated roof. The 460 was the first automobile regularly used by a Pope, and marked the beginning of a relationship between Mercedes-Benz and the Vatican that continues nearly a century later.

As the years passed, the desire to bring the Pope closer to the people grew. Pope John XXIII received a Mercedes-Benz 300d Landaulet with removable rear side windows in 1960. Five years later, Pope Paul VI received a Mercedes-Benz 600 Pullman Landaulet with a raised roof and folding soft top.

In 1980, papal transportation evolved considerably with the Mercedes-Benz 230 G for Pope John Paul II. (That’s right, the Pope had a G-Wagen—more than once.) It was not because the Pope was planning any off-road adventures, but because the raised transparent enclosure at the rear offered protection and visibility. Of all the vehicles used by the Pope over the years, this one may be the most iconic Popemobile. Later additions included an S500 Landaulet in 1997, and specially modified M-Class SUVs in 2002 and 2012.

The exhibit, which opened October 29, also includes an 1886 Benz Patent-Motorwagen and a modern-day S-Class. In addition to the various Popemobiles, visitors can see how Mercedes-Benz vehicles transformed over the last 140 years. The entire collection can be viewed by anyone holding a ticket to tour the Vatican Museums.

#4650. Musk declares Tesla Robotaxi win over Waymo, but Waymo still drives 7x more

Elon Musk says Tesla’s Robotaxi race against Waymo “was never a real contest” after Tesla’s driverless fleet logged 438,000 miles in Austin in a single week, edging past Waymo’s 406,000 weekly average in the city.

That’s one city, one week, and a Waymo figure that’s four months old. Across the US, Waymo still drives about seven times more driverless miles than Tesla every week.

The chart going around comes from Robotaxi Tracker, a community project that pulls driverless mileage from each company’s own reports: Tesla’s weekly Robotaxi safety report and Waymo’s quarterly Safety Impact data hub.

Jason Scharf posted the Austin view on X with the comment that “the battle for Autonomous Austin might already be over.” Musk replied overnight: “It was never a real contest.”

The Austin data is real –albeit with some caveats. In the week ending October 18, Tesla reported 438,000 miles with no safety monitor aboard in Austin, up 30% from the week before. Waymo averaged about 406,000 miles a week in Austin in the second quarter.

But the tracker’s own caption explains the catch. Tesla’s figure is its latest week. Waymo’s is an average of April through June, because Waymo publishes about three months after each quarter ends. So Musk is comparing Tesla’s best week ever to Waymo’s spring.

Switch the same chart to “All markets” and the story flips.

Waymo averaged 3.90 million rider-only miles per week in Q2 2026. Tesla did 558,000 miles in its best week. Waymo’s Phoenix, Bay Area, and Los Angeles markets each drive more miles per week on their own than Tesla’s entire network.

Cumulative numbers are even more lopsided. Waymo has logged 271.3 million rider-only miles since 2020, including 50.7 million in Q2 alone, as we covered when Waymo released its latest safety data. Tesla has 3.11 million driverless miles since January 22, 2026. Waymo drove more than that in a single week.

And Tesla’s total leans almost entirely on one city:

Austin accounts for 79% of Tesla’s weekly driverless miles. Houston, Tampa, Orlando, and Miami combined did about 25,000 miles. Waymo’s smallest tracked market, Atlanta, averaged 250,000 a week in Q2.

The Austin surge has an obvious cause. Tesla launched public Cybercab rides in Austin on September 3.

According to Robotaxi Tracker’s count of the Texas DMV automated-vehicle list, Tesla now has 463 Cybercabs registered in Texas, 337 of them added in the last 30 days. That’s 48% of the 970 autonomous vehicles Tesla has registered in the state.

Tesla isn’t hiding the strategy. On the Q3 earnings call last week, Ashok Elluswamy, Tesla’s head of AI software, said the company wants to “swarm Austin with Cybercabs everywhere.” Musk said the Austin Cybercab fleet had grown “by a factor of 10” in about a month.

So Tesla dumped hundreds of new, company-owned cars into one metro and the miles went up. That’s fleet deployment. It doesn’t show the software can do what Waymo does in 15 cities, and Tesla can’t repeat it everywhere at once.

The bigger problem is what the cars are allowed to do.

On the same earnings call, Elluswamy described the service as constrained by the software, not by regulators. He said that if there’s “the slightest possible risk at all,” Tesla doesn’t take it on, and that the limits are “technology driven” for now. Service hours only recently stretched from 9 p.m. toward 2 a.m., and he listed highways, “higher speed roads,” 24/7 operation, and more weather conditions as things Tesla still has to unlock.

You can see those limits in the rides. Tesla Robotaxis don’t take highways, and riders report they avoid at-grade railroad crossings. In September, a rider had a 10-minute Cybercab trip in Austin turn into a 70-minute detour because the car drove south through East Austin until it found a bridge over the rail line, instead of taking MoPac.

That matters for this comparison, too. Miles is a flattering metric when your car takes the long way. A trip that should cover a few miles and instead loops across town logs a lot more mileage for the same rider.

Waymo, meanwhile, has been taking riders on freeways in Phoenix, San Francisco, and Los Angeles since November 2025.

Credit where it’s due: Tesla’s driverless miles are growing fast, 30% in a single week, and Austin now has a real Tesla fleet carrying the public without anyone in the driver’s seat. A year ago, that wasn’t the case.

I continue to hear tesla refer to its miles as 'driverless miles', but Waymo's as rider only miles. This can be a big difference. Are you sure that this is not an apples and oranges comparison? Do we have confidence that Tesla is only including miles with a rider inside and not driverless miles where the can is spinning circles in a parking lot??

But “never a real contest” is a strange thing to say when you’re behind by 7x on weekly miles and 87x on cumulative miles, and your one win depends on comparing your newest week to your rival’s data from last spring.

What stands out to us is the type of autonomy Tesla is deploying. In 2020, Musk wrote that “Waymo is impressive, but a highly specialized solution,” and that Tesla’s approach was “a general solution.” For years, Tesla fans dismissed Waymo as a geofenced system that only worked in mapped areas with lots of restrictions.

Now look at Tesla’s Robotaxi: geofenced, no highways, avoiding railroad crossings, taking 70 minutes for 10-minute trips, and limited by hours because the software isn’t ready for anything with “the slightest possible risk.” By Musk’s own old definition, that’s a highly specialized solution. Waymo is the one driving on freeways now.

#4649. Obesity in Your 20s and 30s May Increase Cancer Risk Later in Life

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Younger adults with obesity may be more likely to develop cancer before midlife than those who maintain a moderate weight, according to a study published on October 26 in the Annals of Internal Medicine.

The risk for cancer became higher as weight increased. The highest rates were seen in those with severe obesity and abdominal obesity.

This highlights the potential importance of weight management in the prevention of early onset cancer.

Rates of both obesity and early onset cancer are rising among younger adults globally.

This study analyzed data from the Korean National Health Insurance Service database. The researchers identified 6,313,338 adults ages 20 to 39 who had no history of cancer and who underwent standardized national health screenings.

The researchers followed the participants for an average of 11 years.

Body mass index (BMI) was categorized into five groups ranging from underweight to class II obesity using the World Health Organization (WHO) criteria for Asian populations. Waist circumference was also measured as an indicator of abdominal adiposity.

During the analysis, the researchers adjusted for various factors such as:

Over the follow-up period, there were 151,893 cases of cancer among the participants. The incidence rate increased progressively based on obesity categories, from 1.84% in “normal-weight” individuals to 2.24% in class I obesity and 2.62% in class II obesity.

The strongest associations were seen in the following cancers:

Obesity was not associated with breast cancer diagnosed before the age of 50.

Ketan Thanki, MD, board certified colorectal surgeon with the MemorialCare Todd Cancer Institute at Long Beach Medical Center in Long Beach, CA, who wasn’t involved in the study, explained to Healthline that obesity itself causes states that promote cancer formation.

This current study focused on the Korean population. However, the connection between obesity and cancer risk is a global issue.

Previous research has shown that around 10% of all new cancer diagnoses in the United States are associated with obesity. Obesity also accounts for up to 50% of certain cancers, including endometrial and liver cancer.

The study also showed that waist circumference, which indicates abdominal obesity, may be linked to cancer risk that is similar to that of individuals with overweight.

The study researchers used the thresholds set out by the Korean Society for the Study of Obesity. These thresholds put the waist circumference cutoff at over 90 cm (35.4 in) for males and over 85cm (33.46 in) for females.

These are not universal cutoffs. According to the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI), waist circumference measurements that can increase your risk of negative health issues are 101.6 cm (40 in) for males and 88.9 cm (35 in) for females.

Previous research has also suggested an association between waist circumference and cancer risk, independent of BMI. One study showed a potential 11% increased risk of cancer in people with a waist circumference over the thresholds, even if they were physically active.

The current study found that males had a higher relative association between obesity and cancer, while females showed higher absolute risk.

The researchers also found that the absolute risk was higher in adults ages 30 to 39.

Those who currently smoke or who have ever smoked were also found to have a higher risk of developing cancer than those who have never smoked.

“Diet, exercise, and now medications can all be used very effectively to reduce one’s weight and, hopefully as a result, cancer risk,” Thanki said.

He also noted that, due to differences between South Korean populations and those in other countries such as the United States, further studies will be needed to determine how this translates across other populations.

“But I think this trend will likely extend across all cultures,” he said.

#4648. World War II’s baby gas masks are as unnerving as you’d imagine

Published Oct 30, 2026 9:54 AM EDT

Time forgets the vast majority of inventions—usually for good reason. As parents and children everywhere get ready for trick-or-treating, we’d like to turn your attention to one such invention: the baby gas mask.

In the November 1938 issue of Popular Science, “a doll demonstrates the use of the baby gas mask” in an undeniably creepy image. The word mask is perhaps a misnomer here, because this contraption actually completely engulfs the baby as “filtered air is pumped in with an artificial lung.”

These baby gas masks were developed at a time when around the world people feared another world war would—and eventually did—ignite. The brief story on the contraption reads, “Babies are protected from poison gas in case of a wartime attack” by these novel masks.

But it’s still hard to imagine any baby well-behaved enough to sit inside such a creepy invention. Nonetheless, the French inventors behind the technology thought this would be a good idea—even a profitable one. And in the lead up to World War II, the baby gas mask briefly caught on, with several vintage photographs showing off different iterations of the device.

In one 1937 image (featured above), a woman and young toddler both sport gas masks in Germany.

There’s also a whole slew of children and babies wearing gas masks in vintage photographs from England. One photograph (below) shows how a baby gas mask, also known as a hood, worked as a woman demonstrates using the contraption at the historic Holborn Town Hall in London, England.

This particular design took three years to develop. An infant is placed inside a fabric hood featuring a large cellulose acetate window. A drawstring cinches the hood at the infant’s waist, so that the arms, shoulders, and head are completely contained. An adult then operates a rubber bellows to filter air into the hood.

There was apparently no time limit for how long a child could be kept inside the airtight mask—as long as air was steadily pumped in, of course. As to whether the infant enjoyed the contraption, no one could ask.

Another photograph taken (fittingly) during Halloween season, on October 20, 1937, at Dr. Barnardo’s nursery home in Hawkhurst, Kent, England, shows several toddlers in a more traditional face gas mask. The home was actually nicknamed the Babies’ Castle. It originally opened in 1883, after a Mr. Theodore Moillet donated two adjacent mansions and an acre of meadowland for the nursery.

Yet another photograph from England shows several mothers holding babies fitted with the hood-style gas mask designed by the Royal Air Force.

Hospitals in England were also fitted with baby gas masks, and one 1940 photograph shows several nurses testing out the new technology.

One little girl named Jean Panter even convinced her father to make her doll a gas mask. This photograph of little Jean with her doll was taken in England on February 11, 1938, shortly before World War II began. The fact that even a young girl wanted a gas mask for her beloved toy certainly speaks to how much fears of poison gas permeated society before and during World War II.

In 1938, Dr. Jacques Marie Le Mée (sometimes spelled La Mee or Le-Mee), the head physician at the Hôpital Necker-Enfants-Malades in Paris, developed another type of baby gas mask. In fact, the hospital Le Mée worked at is the oldest children’s hospital in the Western world, initially founded in 1801 as Hôpital des Enfants Malades.

In one 1939 photograph, several women and their babies don Le Mée’s baby gas mask in a Parisian square. As opposed to the baby gas hoods on display in vintage English photographs, Le Mée’s invention envelopes the entire baby’s body. Even the baby’s legs will get clean air.

Even though the November 1938 issue of Popular Science says the baby gas mask gracing its pages was developed in France, it’s markedly different to the above photograph of Le Mée’s baby gas mask.

In this design, the window is larger and it’s also unclear how the baby gas mask cinches or becomes airtight around the infant.

Someone holding the child pumps fresh air into the hood-style gas mask. “The person holding the infant controls the amount of fresh air entering the [baby] shelter by pressing on the rubber-lung unit,” the short story in the magazine reads.

But even in dark times, children always find a way to have fun. In one delightful comment on a BBC story about baby gas masks, one reader, William Irwin, remembers having “endless fun playing ‘divers’ with one” baby gas mask.

“We were so far removed from bombing risk areas so I do not believe I was ever put into it as a war-baby. It gave me the interest to eventually become a scuba sports diver.”

Even though this technology thankfully fell by the wayside and seems very strange to modern eyes, it still offers us a lot to think about. The inventions that come out of hard times can even inspire—at least if you’re William Irwin.

#4647. Telltale furrows: What the Baltic Sea seafloor reveals about bottom trawling

To what extent does bottom trawling impact the seafloor of the Baltic Sea—and how quickly does it recover? Two new studies from the Leibniz Institute for Baltic Sea Research Warnemünde (IOW) show that the marks on the seafloor provide a much clearer picture of the actual impact than vessel position data alone. Using high-resolution echo sounder measurements and AI, the researchers reveal previously insufficiently recorded impacts and also document surprisingly rapid changes of the seafloor condition. Furthermore, they found strong indications of fishing violations in a marine protected area. The study results were published in the journals Ecological Informatics and Anthropocene.
