#4646. Do Audi’s Apparent Plans for Scout Factory Production Hint At a Future Off-Road SUV?

In addition to a new factory in Georgia, an Audi official has said the company could build 25,000 units a year of ... something ... at Scout’s South Carolina plant.

Audi CEO Gernot Dollner announced last Saturday that the company plans to open a new factory in Georgia, its first manufacturing facility in America. That plant is set to eventually build 200,000 Q7s, Q8s, and Q9s annually—serious volume for some of Audi’s highest-margin products. That is huge news for the business, but an accompanying detail shared by a U.S. official around the time of the event suggests something that could end up being an even bigger deal for Audi’s lineup of offerings. At least, for off-road enthusiasts.

According to a Reuters report, a U.S. official says that Audi is also planning to build 25,000 vehicles of some sort a year at the new Scout Motors plant in South Carolina. Given that this facility is being built out solely to build the Scout brand’s body-on-frame SUV and truck offerings, this suggests that Audi, too, could be building something more truck-like very soon. And given that the company has also been teasing off-road additions to its lineup since it revealed a Q6 concept equipped with portal axles back in January of 2025, the move would make plenty of sense.

This production plan is in line with a German report from November of last year, which suggested that Audi was planning to build a body-on-frame product at the Scout factory at some point. By utilizing this new platform, Audi could rival the ultra-successful Mercedes-Benz G-Wagen and Land Rover Defender lines with a luxury SUV built from the ground up around off-road capability.

By utilizing existing factory space that would otherwise be used on Scout’s range of electrified off-roaders, Audi could take advantage of existing infrastructure. Perhaps even more importantly, building the trucks in the U.S. would allow Audi to dodge many of President Donald Trump’s heavy tariffs on imported cars, and sell the SUVs at a significantly higher profit margin in an American market with a well-established appetite for go-anywhere luxury SUVs.

#4645. Seven young condors released in northern California

Published Oct 30, 2026 11:12 AM EDT

In 1986, there wasn’t a single California condor (Gymnogyps californianus) left in the wild. Thankfully, it wasn’t because the birds of prey had gone extinct, but they were getting close. In the 1980s, there were fewer than two dozen condors remaining in the wild. That’s why the United States Fish and Wildlife Service moved them into a captive breeding and release program.

Now, the Northern California Condor Restoration Program has released seven young condors into the wild in Yurok Country, close to the Oregon border, according to a statement emailed to Popular Science. One of the birds is particularly special—the condor represents the 200th California condor hatched at the San Diego Zoo Safari Park to be released into the wild. In total, the safari park has hatched 291 condors since 1982.

The seven recently released condors will join 26 other condors already enjoying the Yurok Country site. It’s the most recently established California condor release site, and received its first released condors in 2022. The NCCRP is a collaboration between the Yurok Tribe and the Redwood National and State Parks.

“Condor releases are critical to achieving our ultimate goal- to reestablish a self-sustaining condor population in the wild,” Joe Burnett, California Condor Recovery Program Manager at the Ventana Wildlife Society in California, previously told Popular Science.

It was Burnett that taught us about an unexpected behavior in young condors: the “zoomies” we more frequently associate with dogs.

“We observe the zoomies in both captive and wild condors. It’s just a sudden expression of pure excitement for young condors and very fun to watch,” Burnett explained at the time. “They just can’t contain themselves and totally let loose. They hop, run in circles, or flap around, or all the above! It’s just pure fun!”

It’s unclear whether the special “200th” bird experienced such a display. Either way, the release is happy news. There are now seven more condors in the wild, when only a few years ago there were none.
